title: Grade 5 daily reading
overview: One hundred eighty evenings pair authentic public-domain literature with conversation. Shared reading gradually gives way to an independent first reading, while discussion remains collaborative. Selected novel and myth arcs sit beside whole poems and memoir; each excerpt supplies orientation and explicit boundaries. Allow about fifteen to twenty minutes including rereading and discussion, with flexibility for a family’s pace. Historical language remains visible with brief context where needed. This is a curated sequence, not a measured reading-level certification.

progression.focus: Notice, retell, and support an inference together.
progression.rationale: Shared reading follows extended scenes of friendship and a family move, then tests ideas against lyric images and remembered childhood observations. Readers first distinguish a character’s claim from what the narrator shows.

progression.focus: Track motives and changes across selected scenes.
progression.rationale: Garden, household, and journey episodes require memory of earlier decisions while the context makes each excerpt’s boundaries clear. Poetry rereading brings attention to contrasts and patterns rather than plot alone.

progression.focus: Connect form, imagery, and a developing viewpoint.
progression.rationale: Readers take the first pass independently with shared support for older syntax. Seasonal sonnets and nature writing invite distinctions between observation, personification, and the speaker’s interpretation.

progression.focus: Follow complex causes and compare competing accounts.
progression.rationale: Later railway and homecoming episodes introduce delayed consequences and shifting motives; memoir invites a separate check on remembered evidence. Questions increasingly ask which details support a judgment and which leave room for alternatives.

progression.focus: Test interpretation against language and evidence.
progression.rationale: Myth arcs now reach their central deeds, the slaying of the Gorgon, the winning of the fleece and Theseus’s first fight, which readers follow through cause, consequence and the help heroes receive. Independent reading of compressed poems and remembered experience requires rereading, resolving references and recognizing where figurative claims exceed literal evidence.

progression.focus: Return to shared reading for older prose while defending an interpretation.
progression.rationale: Mary Lamb’s early-nineteenth-century retellings bring long periodic sentences, archaic forms and embedded songs, so most tale nights return to shared reading (17 of the 30 nights are shared) while the poems between them are read independently. Readers explain turning points, qualify claims and use exact language, with an adult available for historical vocabulary and discussion.

days.title: The Wind in the Willows: the riverbank discovery (Chapter I, opening)
days.challenge: Follow a long descriptive sentence and distinguish what Mole observes from the narrator’s playful comparisons.
days.focus: Sound patterns, personification, and the beginning of an unequal friendship.
days.context: Mole leaves his underground spring cleaning and encounters a river for the first time. This is the opening of the novel; the animals behave as people while retaining animal features.

excerpt.locator: The Wind in the Willows: the riverbank discovery (Chapter I, opening); source text begins "The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First wit" and ends "f and took to the sculls again. "Do you know, I've never been in a boat before in all my life."".

questions.prompt: How does the repeated scraping language make Mole’s arrival above ground feel?
facilitatorNotes: Read the sequence aloud slowly, then faster. Its repeated consonants and reversed order suggest effort followed by the sudden release of pop.
evidence: scraped and scratched and scrabbled and scrooged

questions.prompt: Why is the river described as a storyteller rather than simply a body of water?
facilitatorNotes: Its chatter and movement fascinate an inexperienced Mole. The comparison lets readers share his wonder; it is not a literal claim that water speaks.
evidence: a babbling procession of the best stories in the world

questions.prompt: What does Rat do that an invitation alone cannot do for Mole?
facilitatorNotes: Rat brings a boat and supports Mole as he enters. Practical assistance bridges the gap between his experience and Mole’s uncertainty.
evidence: Then he held up his fore-paw

days.title: The Wind in the Willows: Rat’s world (Chapter I, continued)
days.challenge: Recognize comic exaggeration while following Rat’s long speeches.
days.focus: A character’s enthusiasm, hospitality, and limited viewpoint.
days.context: Mole has just entered Rat’s boat and admitted that he has never been boating. Rat now describes the activity he loves; an illustration between installments is not reproduced.

excerpt.locator: The Wind in the Willows: Rat’s world (Chapter I, continued); source text begins ""What?" cried the Rat, open-mouthed: "Never been in a--you never--well I--what have you been do" and ends "he bed of it and find fresh food to eat, and things careless people have dropped out of boats!"".

questions.prompt: How does the collision interrupt and also confirm Rat’s speech about boats?
facilitatorNotes: He runs into the bank while praising boating, then continues without losing enthusiasm. The action makes his total absorption comic.
evidence: The boat struck the bank full tilt.

questions.prompt: What effect does the nearly unbroken list of food have?
facilitatorNotes: It makes the basket seem overflowing and Rat’s recital rapid. Mole calls it too much, while Rat calls it his usual provision; compare their expectations.
evidence: coldtonguecoldhamcoldbeefpickledgherkinssaladfrenchrollscresssandwiches

questions.prompt: What does Rat mean by calling the river brother, sister, and company?
facilitatorNotes: The river fills emotional and practical roles in his life. Readers may admire his attachment while questioning his claim that nothing beyond it is worthwhile.
evidence: It's brother and sister to me

days.title: The Wind in the Willows: boundaries of Rat’s knowledge (Chapter I, continued)
days.challenge: Separate a speaker’s confident judgment from the experience supporting it.
days.focus: Contrasts between curiosity, loyalty to home, and unfamiliar places.
days.context: Rat has described the river as his whole world. Mole asks about its neighbors and the places beyond it as they approach their picnic spot.

excerpt.locator: The Wind in the Willows: boundaries of Rat’s knowledge (Chapter I, continued); source text begins ""But isn't it a bit dull at times?" the Mole ventured to ask. "Just you and the river, and no o" and ends "so very beautiful that the Mole could only hold up both fore-paws and gasp: "O my! O my! O my!"".

questions.prompt: Why is Mole’s question about loneliness surprising to Rat?
facilitatorNotes: Rat describes a crowded bank full of neighbors and obligations. Mole imagines an isolated river life because he has only just arrived.
evidence: The bank is so crowded nowadays

questions.prompt: Does Rat’s dismissal of the Wide World rest on firsthand experience?
facilitatorNotes: No: he says he has never been there. Discuss how confidence and familiarity differ from evidence, without assuming all his warnings are false.
evidence: I've never been there

questions.prompt: How does the backwater description answer the anxious conversation without an argument?
facilitatorNotes: The quiet beauty absorbs Mole’s attention. Water, roots, wheel, and sounds show why the river world attracts Rat even while his wider judgments remain limited.
evidence: a soothing murmur of sound

days.title: The Wind in the Willows: picnic manners (Chapter I, continued)
days.challenge: Track several speakers and infer a comic rule from repeated behavior.
days.focus: Hospitality, social awkwardness, and the difference between pleasure and cleanup.
days.context: Rat and Mole stop at a sheltered backwater for lunch. New visitors and stories introduce the social habits of the riverbank.

excerpt.locator: The Wind in the Willows: picnic manners (Chapter I, continued); source text begins "The Rat brought the boat alongside the bank, made her fast, helped the still awkward Mole safel" and ends "ithout knowing it--still, somehow, the thing got finished at last, without much loss of temper.".

questions.prompt: Compare Badger’s arrival with Otter’s: how do their words and actions establish different temperaments?
facilitatorNotes: Otter joins and talks, while Badger notices company and leaves. Avoid deciding either is simply good or bad; the scene distinguishes social preferences.
evidence: Why didn't you invite me, Ratty?
H'm! Company

questions.prompt: What double meaning makes Otter’s comment about Toad’s stability funny?
facilitatorNotes: Stability refers both to sticking with an interest and staying balanced in a boat. Rat’s list of abandoned hobbies supplies the first meaning; Toad’s rowing supplies the second.
evidence: but no stability--especially in a boat!

questions.prompt: Why is repacking the basket a useful ending to the picnic scene?
facilitatorNotes: It contrasts delighted unpacking with overlooked plates, fork, and mustard. Mole’s persistence keeps the mishaps light and shows his determination to enjoy the day.
evidence: Packing the basket was not quite such pleasant work as unpacking the basket.

days.title: The Wind in the Willows: confidence and the overturned boat (Chapter I, continued)
days.challenge: Follow rapid action while distinguishing confidence from demonstrated ability.
days.focus: Foreshadowing, consequences, and a friend’s immediate response.
days.context: After the picnic, Mole feels increasingly at home in Rat’s boat. Rat has not yet taught him to row.
days.contentNote: An animal character briefly struggles in water before being rescued.

excerpt.locator: The Wind in the Willows: confidence and the overturned boat (Chapter I, continued); source text begins "The afternoon sun was getting low as the Rat sculled gently homewards in a dreamy mood, murmuri" and ends "animal to shore, hauled him out, and set him down on the bank, a squashy, pulpy lump of misery.".

questions.prompt: What warning does the parenthesis “so he thought” give the reader?
facilitatorNotes: It separates Mole’s belief that he is competent from the narrator’s assessment. The ensuing accident confirms that feeling at home is not a lesson in rowing.
evidence: so he thought

questions.prompt: Which decision turns Mole’s wish to row into the accident?
facilitatorNotes: He grabs the sculls before learning and displaces Rat. The problem is not merely asking to learn; it is acting as though the skill is already his.
evidence: He jumped up and seized the sculls

questions.prompt: How do the repeated sensations change the pace after the boat overturns?
facilitatorNotes: Coldness, sinking, brightness, and coughing make the event immediate and frightening before Rat’s grip ends it. A response should name details rather than reduce the passage to a moral.
evidence: How bright and welcome the sun looked

days.title: The Wind in the Willows: making room for a learner (Chapter I, ending)
days.challenge: Explain character relationships through offers, gestures, and changes in tone.
days.focus: Forgiveness that includes practical teaching rather than denial of a mistake.
days.context: Rat has rescued Mole after Mole’s untrained attempt to row overturned their boat. This installment finishes the novel’s first chapter, not the complete novel.

excerpt.locator: The Wind in the Willows: making room for a learner (Chapter I, ending); source text begins "When the Rat had rubbed him down a bit, and wrung some of the wet out of him, he said, "Now the" and ends "s he caught, at intervals, something of what the wind went whispering so constantly among them.".

questions.prompt: What does Mole’s concern for the luncheon basket add to his apology?
facilitatorNotes: It shows comic attachment to the day’s pleasures and recognition that his actions affected Rat’s belongings. His apology can be sincere and still comically disproportionate.
evidence: how I might have lost that beautiful luncheon-basket

questions.prompt: Why is Rat’s offer to teach rowing and swimming more helpful than simply saying everything is fine?
facilitatorNotes: He forgives the mistake while addressing Mole’s missing skills. The offer turns dependence into an opportunity to learn.
evidence: And I'll teach you to row and to swim

questions.prompt: How does Rat preserve Mole’s dignity when Mole becomes tearful?
facilitatorNotes: He looks away rather than calling attention to the tears. Connect this small gesture with the larger welcome at his home.
evidence: But the Rat kindly looked in another direction

days.title: The Railway Children: an ordinary home and an extraordinary engine
days.challenge: Hear the narrator’s teasing voice and distinguish an actual event from its comic retelling.
days.focus: How a broken toy reveals affection and hints at a larger change.
days.context: Meet Roberta (also called Bobbie), Peter and Phyllis before a family change. Their mother writes stories and playful poems.
days.contentNote: The narrator jokes about the old expectation that boys should hide tears.

excerpt.locator:
Chapter I, opening through Mother’s engine poem; opens “THEY were not railway children to begin with. I don't suppose they had ever thought about railways e”; closes “re rather red,
His cold must just excuse it:
Offer him pie; you may be sure
He never will refuse it.”.

questions.prompt: Which details make this family seem fortunate before the engine breaks?
facilitatorNotes: Readers can cite comforts, but should also notice Mother’s availability and Father’s fairness; wealth and attention are distinct kinds of good fortune.
evidence: She was almost always there, ready to play with the children

questions.prompt: Why is “boys of ten do not cry” unlikely to be a plain statement of fact here?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator has just mentioned Peter’s hurt feelings and reported tears. The exaggerated denial gently imitates Peter’s wish to seem grown up; other readings should account for both clues.
evidence: The others said he cried over it,—but of course boys of ten do not cry

questions.prompt: How does Mother’s poem turn Peter’s distress into affectionate comedy?
facilitatorNotes: The poem treats the toy accident as a grand tragedy but ends with his reliable appetite. Reread the shift from “miserable fate” to accepting pie; it teases rather than dismisses him.
evidence:
Offer him pie; you may be sure
He never will refuse it.

days.title: The Railway Children: the interrupted repair
days.challenge: Track an abrupt change of mood through dialogue, sound and physical detail.
days.focus: What the children can infer without being told the bad news.
days.context: Peter hopes Father can mend the damaged toy engine. Two visitors interrupt the family evening.
days.contentNote: A parent leaves unexpectedly and the family is distressed; the passage does not yet explain why.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Father’s return through Roberta’s silent promise; opens “Father had been away in the country for three or four days. All Peter's hopes for the curing of his ”; closes “f as she heard through the dark the catching of her Mother's breath, “we won't know it. That's all.””.

questions.prompt: How does Father combine reassurance with a realistic repair plan?
facilitatorNotes: He offers hope but names materials and time: solder or brazing, a valve and a Saturday afternoon. His answer is comforting because it includes a practicable next step.
evidence: a bit of brazing, say, or some solder, and a new valve

questions.prompt: Which changes tell the reader that the visitors’ business is serious before anyone explains it?
facilitatorNotes: Father’s voice becomes unusually loud, the visit lasts, and Mother returns pale. Readers should distinguish these observations from Ruth’s unconfirmed guesses.
evidence: Father's voice sounded louder and different

questions.prompt: What does Roberta’s choice to stay still suggest about her relationship with Mother?
facilitatorNotes: She notices the crying but protects Mother’s wish not to discuss it. Her silence is attentive care rather than failure to notice; another interpretation needs evidence from her thought.
evidence: If Mother doesn't want us to know she's been crying

days.title: The Railway Children: promises and small acts
days.challenge: Notice contrasts between a promise, an immediate action and a revealing joke.
days.focus: How the siblings begin to turn worry into practical kindness.
days.context: Father has left after a troubling visit. Mother asks the children for help while keeping the reason private.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, the next morning through “Everything’s perfectly horrid”; opens “When they came down to breakfast the next morning, Mother had already gone out.”; closes “ever wanted things to happen to make Mother unhappy,” said Roberta. “Everything's perfectly horrid.””.

questions.prompt: How do the children help Mother before she asks them to behave well?
facilitatorNotes: Each child performs a small task: removing hat-pins or gloves, bringing slippers, or easing her headache. They already show care physically, even while earlier arguing.
evidence: Peter unfastened her walking-shoes and fetched her soft velvety slippers for her.

questions.prompt: Why does Peter admit that he asked Ruth about the trouble? What makes the admission difficult?
facilitatorNotes: He has already been challenged by Bobbie, and Mother now asks them not to question others. His cringing and shuffled feet show discomfort, yet he confesses rather than hiding the earlier question.
evidence: I did ask Ruth

questions.prompt: What different ideas of “being good” do Peter, Phyllis and the girls’ final action reveal?
facilitatorNotes: Peter postpones goodness until tomorrow; Phyllis includes present feelings and speech; the girls find a concrete action in folding clothes. The humor exposes how a large promise must become small choices.
evidence: which was the only way of being good that they could think of.

days.title: The Railway Children: choosing what to take
days.challenge: Compare outward excitement with another character’s less visible feelings.
days.focus: Useful possessions and the difference between cheerfulness and ease.
days.context: The family prepares to leave its comfortable London home. The children still do not know the full reason.
days.contentNote: Includes a brief account of a servant hitting Peter and a minor hand injury, without graphic description.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, the difficult weeks through Roberta’s admiration of Mother; opens “Everything continued to be perfectly horrid for some weeks.”; closes “how brave you are! How I love you! Fancy being brave enough to laugh when you're feeling like that!””.

questions.prompt: Why does the list of packed objects tell us this is unlike a holiday?
facilitatorNotes: Chairs, bedsteads, kitchenware and fire-irons are being moved. These are daily-life necessities, so the whole household is relocating rather than taking a short trip.
evidence: All sorts of things were packed that you don't pack when you go to the seaside.

questions.prompt: How does Mother answer Roberta’s complaint about taking “ugly things”?
facilitatorNotes: She changes the standard from beauty to usefulness and softens the financial change by calling it play. Discuss whether this comfort also conceals how serious the move is.
evidence: We're taking the useful ones

questions.prompt: Why does Roberta call Mother brave after Mother laughs at Peter’s enthusiasm?
facilitatorNotes: Roberta sees the face Mother turns away and senses that the laugh costs effort. The passage distinguishes bravery from feeling happy; Peter and Bobbie read the same moment differently.
evidence: Fancy being brave enough to laugh when you're feeling like that!

days.title: The Railway Children: a dark arrival
days.challenge: Build atmosphere from several senses while noticing the narrator’s glimpse of the future.
days.focus: How a disappointing arrival can begin a different life.
days.context: The family has packed its useful household things and travelled to a new country house. They arrive late at night.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, departure by cab through the end of the chapter; opens “Next day boxes were filled, and boxes and more boxes; and then late in the afternoon a cab came to t”; closes ““Only the rats!” said Peter, in the dark.”.

questions.prompt: Which details make the journey from station to house uncomfortable rather than adventurous?
facilitatorNotes: Cold noses, the tight hat elastic, undone laces, mud and gritty wheels turn travel into bodily discomfort. Readers may choose different details if they explain their effect.
evidence: the gritty crunch of its wheels

questions.prompt: What does the narrator know about the railway that the children cannot yet know?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says it will become dear and central to them, while they only feel cold. That gap invites readers to expect a changed relationship rather than treating this arrival as the final judgment.
evidence: it would become the centre of their new life

questions.prompt: How do the final sounds and the extinguished candle produce the chapter’s ending?
facilitatorNotes: The bare room first defeats expectations of warmth; rustling raises fear, the cart man names rats, and the door’s draught removes the small light. Phyllis’s knocked chair ends the scene in confused darkness.
evidence: the sudden draught of it blew out the candle.

days.title: Palanquin Bearers
days.challenge: Compare several similes without assuming they all express exactly the same feeling.
days.focus: Rhythm and shifting images of lightness, movement, and emotion.
days.context: A palanquin is a carried seat or litter. Naidu writes in the collective voice of its bearers, who compare the bride they carry to a flower, a bird, a star and a pearl.

excerpt.locator:
Palanquin Bearers; source text begins "Lightly, O lightly we bear her along,
She sways like a flower in the wind of our song;
She skim" and ends "f a bride.
Lightly, O lightly we glide and we sing,
We bear her along like a pearl on a string.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Golden_Threshold/Folk_Songs/Palanquin-Bearers

questions.prompt: How does the repeated lightly or softly influence a read-aloud?
facilitatorNotes: It invites a gentle rocking rhythm, reinforced by glide and bear. Try two deliveries and explain which words each emphasizes.
evidence: Lightly, O lightly

questions.prompt: How do the flower and pearl comparisons differ?
facilitatorNotes: The flower emphasizes swaying delicacy; the pearl suggests preciousness and being held along a line. Other evidence-based interpretations are welcome.
evidence: She sways like a flower
like a pearl on a string

questions.prompt: Why might the tear image complicate the poem’s otherwise buoyant motion?
facilitatorNotes: A bride’s tear can suggest mixed feelings amid celebration. The text permits emotional complexity without specifying a single private reason.
evidence: She falls like a tear from the eyes of a bride.

days.title: Wandering Singers
days.challenge: Connect recurring wind imagery to the speakers’ idea of home.
days.focus: A roaming community, remembered stories, and the costs of not staying.
days.context: The parenthetical source note says this was written to one of the singers’ tunes. Lays means songs, and tarry means stay. These are imagined collective speakers in Naidu’s English poem.

excerpt.locator:
Wandering Singers; source text begins "Where the voice of the wind calls our wandering feet,
Through echoing forest and echoing street" and ends "go.
No love bids us tarry, no joy bids us wait:
The voice of the wind is the voice of our fate.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Golden_Threshold/Folk_Songs/Wandering_Singers

questions.prompt: How can the speakers call the world home while continuing to wander?
facilitatorNotes: They claim kinship beyond one settled place. Discuss whether this sounds freeing, lonely, or both, using the repeated movement.
evidence: All men are our kindred, the world is our home.

questions.prompt: What range of experiences do their songs preserve?
facilitatorNotes: The second stanza includes faded cities, past people, battles, kings, and ordinary happiness and sorrow. Their repertoire connects public history with personal feeling.
evidence: And happy and simple and sorrowful things.

questions.prompt: Does the final stanza make wandering sound entirely chosen?
facilitatorNotes: The wind becomes fate, while love and joy cannot hold them. This can suggest freedom or a force they follow; either reading needs the final wording.
evidence: The voice of the wind is the voice of our fate.

days.title: Indian Weavers
days.challenge: Trace a symbolic life sequence through time of day, color, and repeated questions.
days.focus: How a compact three-stanza structure holds birth, marriage, and death.
days.context: Halcyon names a brightly colored bird; a shroud is a burial cloth. The poem arranges three exchanges between a questioner and weavers.
days.contentNote: The final stanza names death and a burial cloth without graphic description.

excerpt.locator:
Indian Weavers; source text begins "Weavers, weaving at break of day,
Why do you weave a garment so gay? . . .
Blue as the wing of " and ends "ght chill? . . .
White as a feather and white as a cloud,
We weave a dead man's funeral shroud.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Golden_Threshold/Folk_Songs/Indian_Weavers

questions.prompt: What changes when the question about a gay garment becomes a question about moonlight chill?
facilitatorNotes: The opening is bright and lively; the final question becomes quiet and solemn. Time and tone prepare the different purpose of the cloth.
evidence: a garment so gay
the moonlight chill

questions.prompt: How do the three cloths create a larger sequence than one working day?
facilitatorNotes: Newborn robes, marriage veils, and a funeral shroud trace stages of life. The day’s hours serve as a pattern rather than a literal claim that one life lasts a day.
evidence: new-born child
marriage-veils
funeral shroud

questions.prompt: Why might white be compared with both a feather and a cloud?
facilitatorNotes: Both images are pale and light, softening the ending’s visual field while the shroud names death directly. Avoid insisting that the color has only one universal meaning.
evidence: White as a feather and white as a cloud

days.title: Coromandel Fishers
days.challenge: Hold affection for shore and enthusiasm for sea together rather than treating them as a contradiction.
days.focus: Collective voice, personification, and persuasive invitation.
days.context: The Coromandel is an Indian coastal region. Catamarans here are fishing craft. The fishermen speak together, calling the sea their mother and the cloud their brother.

excerpt.locator:
Coromandel Fishers; source text begins "Rise, brothers, rise, the wakening skies pray to the morning lights
The wind lies asleep in the" and ends "foam's glee:
Row, brothers, row to the blue of the verge, where the low sky mates with the sea.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Golden_Threshold/Folk_Songs/Coromandel_Fishers

questions.prompt: How does the opening turn weather into a family scene?
facilitatorNotes: The wind rests in dawn’s arms like a child. The comparison softens the morning and prepares a confident departure.
evidence: like a child that has cried all night

questions.prompt: What is the effect of making sea, cloud, and waves family or companions?
facilitatorNotes: The speakers present their work environment as a community they belong to. This expresses attachment, not literal kinship or proof that storms cannot harm them.
evidence: The sea is our mother, the cloud is our brother

questions.prompt: Why list the shore’s sweetness before calling the spray sweeter?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison acknowledges genuine comforts being left behind. Their preference gains force because the alternative is attractive rather than dismissed.
evidence: But sweeter, O brothers, the kiss of the spray

days.title: Spring announces itself — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Use the dialogue around unfamiliar Yorkshire words to follow the gardener’s explanation.
days.focus: Spring imagery connects changes in the weather with Mary’s growing attention.
days.context: Mary Lennox, orphaned when cholera killed her parents and most of their household in India, now lives at her uncle’s house, Misselthwaite Manor, and has heard of a garden locked for ten years. She goes outside after a storm and talks with the gardener Ben Weatherstaff.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, The Key of the Garden; begins "Mary felt lonelier than ever when she knew she was no longer in the house. She went out into the gar"; ends "ulders toward the robin. "He's the only one as knows. No one else has seen inside it for ten year'."". Complete source paragraphs 424–440 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does running change Mary’s mood before Ben speaks to her?
facilitatorNotes: She feels lonely when Martha leaves, but counting ten circuits and noticing the bright sky improves her spirits. Her mood changes through an action before anyone reassures her.
evidence: when she had finished she felt in better spirits

questions.prompt: Ben says the earth is in a good humor. What details turn that description into a picture of approaching spring?
facilitatorNotes: He describes warming sun, green spikes underground and gradual unfolding leaves. The personification makes the earth seem busy rather than lifeless; readers can identify several supporting details.
evidence: It's in a good humor makin' ready to grow things.

questions.prompt: Why is Ben’s answer about the locked garden less helpful than his answer about bulbs?
facilitatorNotes: He willingly describes ordinary growth, but redirects Mary to the robin when she asks about the roses. His change to a surly manner suggests a guarded subject rather than a lack of all gardening knowledge.
evidence: He's the only one as knows. No one else has seen inside it for ten year'.

days.title: A friend uncovers a key — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Separate what the narrator explains from what Mary herself knows.
days.focus: An apparently ordinary bird encounter becomes a discovery through observation.
days.context: Ben has just said that no person has seen inside the locked garden for ten years. Mary returns to the ivy-covered wall where the robin often appears.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, The Key of the Garden; begins "Ten years was a long time, Mary thought. She had been born ten years ago."; ends "aps it has been buried for ten years," she said in a whisper. "Perhaps it is the key to the garden!"". Complete source paragraphs 441–450 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary count the robin among the people she likes?
facilitatorNotes: She treats its following, chirping and willingness to approach as signs of companionship. The passage shows her expanding capacity to care, even though a bird is not literally a person.
evidence: She thought of the robin as one of the people.

questions.prompt: What caused the earth to be disturbed, and does Mary know that cause?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator tells us a dog dug for a mole. Mary sees the hole without knowing why it is there; readers have information she lacks.
evidence: Mary looked at it, not really knowing why the hole was there

questions.prompt: Does the final sentence prove that the key opens the garden? How does its wording create suspense?
facilitatorNotes: No. Mary repeats perhaps, making a promising inference from the key’s age rather than demonstrating it. The question of the door remains open.
evidence: Perhaps it is the key to the garden!

days.title: A secret place imagined — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Track the narrator’s explanation of a change Mary does not yet understand.
days.focus: Imagination and curiosity develop before the hidden door is found.
days.context: Mary has found an old key. She does not yet know where the garden door is or whether the key fits it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, The Robin Who Showed the Way; begins "She looked at the key quite a long time. She turned it over and over, and thought about it. As I hav"; ends "y it with her when she went out, so that if she ever should find the hidden door she would be ready.". Complete source paragraphs 453–455 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What attracts Mary to the garden besides its possible flowers?
facilitatorNotes: Its long closure promises strangeness, privacy and a place for her own play. Several interpretations of this desire are possible, but they should distinguish curiosity from wanting beautiful roses only.
evidence: she could make up some play of her own and play it quite alone

questions.prompt: How does the narrator connect movement of Mary’s body with movement of her mind?
facilitatorNotes: The moor air and wind are described as stirring her blood and mind. This parallel presents physical activity and curiosity as growing together in the story, not as a universal medical explanation.
evidence: so the same things had stirred her mind

questions.prompt: Why is keeping the key in her pocket a small but important decision?
facilitatorNotes: She cannot solve the ivy-covered-door problem yet, but prepares for the chance of finding it. Her disappointment turns into a practical intention rather than giving up.
evidence: so that if she ever should find the hidden door she would be ready.

days.title: The ivy curtain moves — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Follow the chain of small actions that makes a discovery possible.
days.focus: Pacing and repeated words heighten the moment of entering the garden.
days.context: Martha has given Mary a skipping rope. Mary carries the old key while exploring near the garden wall; she still cannot see a door.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, The Robin Who Showed the Way; begins "Mary skipped round all the gardens and round the orchard, resting every few minutes. At length she w"; ends "She was standing _inside_ the secret garden.". Complete source paragraphs 498–507 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What has Mary achieved with the rope, and how does she react when she must stop?
facilitatorNotes: She has reached thirty skips and laughs with pleasure despite being breathless. The passage treats practice and partial progress as satisfying rather than showing failure.
evidence: She did not mind much, because she had already counted up to thirty.

questions.prompt: What roles do the robin and the gust of wind play in finding the door?
facilitatorNotes: The robin draws her near the ivy; the gust moves the leaves and exposes a knob. Mary then investigates. Calling it Magic is her interpretation of a chain the narrator also describes physically.
evidence: a round knob which had been covered by the leaves hanging over it

questions.prompt: How does the writing make opening the door feel slow even though Mary is eager?
facilitatorNotes: Two hands, long breaths, looking behind her, and the repeated slowly delay the arrival. The brief final sentence gives release after those delays.
evidence: the door which opened slowly--slowly.

days.title: Alone without loneliness — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish detailed visual evidence from Mary’s uncertainty about whether plants are alive.
days.focus: The description makes a neglected garden both mysterious and welcoming.
days.context: Mary has opened the hidden door and stepped into the neglected garden for the first time.
