The high walls which shut "; ends "quite alive garden, how wonderful it would be, and what thousands of roses would grow on every side!". Complete source paragraphs 510–518 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How have the climbing roses changed the shape of the garden?
facilitatorNotes: Their tendrils form curtains, bridges and arches between trees rather than remaining in neat separate beds. Those comparisons make natural growth seem like unusual architecture.
evidence: made lovely bridges of themselves

questions.prompt: Why can Mary not settle whether the roses are dead simply by looking around?
facilitatorNotes: She sees bare gray and brown branches but lacks Ben’s knowledge. The narrator explicitly separates an expert’s possible judgment from her limited observations.
evidence: If she had been Ben Weatherstaff she could have told whether the wood was alive

questions.prompt: How can Mary seem hundreds of miles from everyone without feeling lonely?
facilitatorNotes: The robin accompanies her and she feels ownership, wonder and a new purpose. Accept different emphases supported by these details; physical solitude and emotional loneliness are not identical here.
evidence: somehow she did not feel lonely at all.

days.title: Making room to breathe — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Trace how one observation leads to an improvised gardening method.
days.focus: Mary’s first useful work transforms her relationship with a place.
days.context: Inside the hidden garden, Mary still fears that the roses may be dead. She begins to look closely at the ground.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, The Strangest House Any One Ever Lived In; begins "Her skipping-rope had hung over her arm when she came in and after she had walked about for a while "; ends "in'!" she said. "Eh! mother will be pleased when I tell her what th' skippin'-rope's done for thee."". Complete source paragraphs 519–533 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What changes Mary’s claim about the garden from uncertainty to hope?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes pale green points and searches for more. Even if the roses are dead, the new growth establishes that some life remains.
evidence: Even if the roses are dead, there are other things alive.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary clear grass around the shoots even though she knows little about gardening?
facilitatorNotes: She notices that thick grass seems to crowd tiny plants and uses a sharp piece of wood to open spaces. Her method begins in close observation and care rather than formal instruction.
evidence: they did not seem to have room enough to grow

questions.prompt: Why does Martha credit the skipping rope for Mary’s appetite while readers know more?
facilitatorNotes: Martha sees Mary’s appearance and dinner but has not seen her hours of digging. This gap preserves the garden secret and gives readers another explanation for Mary’s hunger.
evidence: what th' skippin'-rope's done for thee.

days.title: Questions beneath the soil — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Infer the question beneath Mary’s indirect questions while keeping two characters’ knowledge separate.
days.focus: Practical knowledge passes through family conversation, with a secret shaping what Mary says.
days.context: At dinner after secretly digging, Mary asks Martha about an onion-like root and begins planning how to get proper tools.
days.contentNote: The novel uses the colonial term “natives” in Mary’s recollection of India, reflecting the narrator’s period.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, The Strangest House Any One Ever Lived In; begins "In the course of her digging with her pointed stick Mistress Mary had found herself digging up a sor"; ends "earns something besides her A B C. Children's as good as 'rithmetic to set you findin' out things.'"". Complete source paragraphs 534–550 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why is Martha’s description of bulbs as things that help themselves important to Mary?
facilitatorNotes: Mary worries about plants neglected for years. Martha’s account of long-lived bulbs spreading underground offers hope that the garden can survive without constant help.
evidence: They're things as helps themselves

questions.prompt: How does Mary explain wanting a spade without revealing the garden?
facilitatorNotes: She describes loneliness and a wish to dig somewhere, omitting that she already has a specific hidden place. Her words are shaped by fear of losing the garden.
evidence: She must be careful if she meant to keep her secret kingdom.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison between children and arithmetic suggest about Martha’s mother?
facilitatorNotes: Raising children has taught her to notice needs and solve practical problems. The image credits experience as a kind of thinking, rather than dismissing her because her knowledge is not bookish.
evidence: Children's as good as 'rithmetic to set you findin' out things.

days.title: A letter begins a partnership — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Read a letter embedded in dialogue and identify what each character contributes to the plan.
days.focus: Writing turns a private wish into a practical collaboration.
days.context: Mary wants tools and seeds for the hidden garden. Martha suggests that her brother Dickon could buy them in the village.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, The Strangest House Any One Ever Lived In; begins ""How much would a spade cost--a little one?" Mary asked."; ends ""Yes, I do. I never saw a boy foxes and crows loved. I want to see him very much."". Complete source paragraphs 551–575 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How do Mary and Martha view the same amount of money differently?
facilitatorNotes: Mary has money she has not known how to spend; Martha relates it to cottage rent that is hard to find. The contrast reveals different household circumstances rather than a mathematical disagreement.
evidence: Tha' can buy anything in th' world tha' wants.

questions.prompt: Why must the message to Dickon be printed, and how do the girls manage that requirement?
facilitatorNotes: Dickon reads print rather than handwriting. Martha provides materials and dictates; Mary discovers she can form printed letters by trying. Their abilities combine.
evidence: Our Dickon can only read printin'.

questions.prompt: Why does the letter ask for seeds that are both pretty and easy to grow?
facilitatorNotes: Mary is a beginner, so success depends on choosing suitable plants as well as attractive ones. The instruction makes the purchase a thoughtful plan rather than merely buying many seeds.
evidence: Pick the prettiest ones and easy to grow because she has never done it before

days.title: Ben’s guarded delight — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Interpret tone by comparing a character’s spoken teasing with physical reactions.
days.focus: The robin exposes affection beneath Ben’s gruff manner.
days.context: Mary has spent a week of sunshine working secretly in the garden and often seeks out Ben Weatherstaff. The narrator compares her new manner with the way she first spoke to him.
days.contentNote: Ben makes blunt comments about Mary’s body and appearance. The narrator traces Mary’s first manner toward Ben to the way she was taught to command servants in colonial India, using the period words “native” and “salaam.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Dickon; begins "During that week of sunshine, she became more intimate with Ben Weatherstaff. She surprised him seve"; ends "But because he kept breaking into a slow grin now and then, Mary was not afraid to talk to him.". Complete source paragraphs 597–615 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: The narrator says Ben “did not know” how Mary had first spoken to him. What had Mary learned in India, and how has her manner changed?
facilitatorNotes: She had spoken to him as she would to a servant who must obey; now she is more civil and approaches quietly because she wants his company. The narrator presents her old habit as something she is unlearning.
evidence: Then, also, she was more civil than she had been.
accustomed to salaam to his masters

questions.prompt: Why does Ben compare Mary to the robin?
facilitatorNotes: Both appear unexpectedly near him. What sounds like a complaint also acknowledges that Mary has become a familiar visitor. Readers may hear affection or irritation, but should use the comparison itself.
evidence: I never knows when I shall see thee or which side tha'll come from.

questions.prompt: Which actions contradict Ben’s teasing claim that the robin is only showing off?
facilitatorNotes: He tries not to appear pleased, then stands almost without breathing so as not to frighten the bird. Those gestures reveal tenderness behind sarcastic speech.
evidence: as if he would not have stirred for the world, lest his robin should start away

questions.prompt: How does the bird’s visit change what Mary feels able to do next?
facilitatorNotes: She sees Ben repeatedly grin and becomes unafraid to talk. The bird serves as a bridge between two people as well as being Ben’s companion.
evidence: Mary was not afraid to talk to him.

days.title: Roses and an unfinished memory — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Combine reluctant statements to infer a relationship that is not fully explained.
days.focus: Gardening knowledge and grief emerge together in a guarded conversation.
days.context: The robin has softened Ben’s mood. Mary uses the opportunity to ask how she might grow flowers while keeping her discovery secret.
days.contentNote: The passage briefly mentions a woman’s death and Ben’s grief; it contains no description of the death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Dickon; begins ""Have you a garden of your own?" she asked."; ends " make him talk to her. Also she began to believe that he knew everything in the world about flowers.". Complete source paragraphs 616–646 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What leads Ben from naming practical vegetables to talking about roses?
facilitatorNotes: Mary asks specifically about a flower garden, then follows his mention of roses. His explanation introduces a woman who loved them and taught him to care for them.
evidence: She had a lot in a place she was fond of

questions.prompt: What does Ben admit doing after the woman died, and why does that matter for the roses?
facilitatorNotes: He returned once or twice a year to prune and dig because he cared for her and the plants. The detail complicates the idea that the roses were completely abandoned.
evidence: Once or twice a year I'd go an' work at 'em a bit

questions.prompt: Why does Mary like Ben even after he sends her away sharply?
facilitatorNotes: She has received knowledge, attention and hints of sympathy. His crossness does not erase what she has learned about him; readers can distinguish friendliness of manner from deeper care.
evidence: she liked in spite of his crossness.

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: a lake garden and the first spring flower
days.challenge: Follow a shift from mapped surroundings to close description and personification.
days.focus: How close observation becomes admiration for wild plants.
days.context: John Muir looks back on the Wisconsin farm where he lived as a boy after moving from Scotland. This is his remembered perspective, written many years later.
days.contentNote: Muir uses Christian language and a European settler’s viewpoint, and recalls nibbling plant seeds during long sermons.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Fountain Lake through the pasque-flower account; opens “Our beautiful lake, named Fountain Lake by father, but Muir’s Lake by the neighbors, is one of the m”; closes “ nibbled while the discourses were at their dullest kept us awake and filled our minds with flowers.”.

questions.prompt: How does Muir arrange the lake’s plants so a reader can picture their positions?
facilitatorNotes: He moves from springs and surrounding hills toward successive zones: rushes and then a wide band of lilies. These spatial details give the glowing scene a physical structure.
evidence: just beyond the rushes a zone of white and orange water-lilies

questions.prompt: Why does he compare a wild lake with a cultivated lily garden?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison reverses an expectation that cultivated gardens are superior: he finds the lake’s abundance more impressive. Link the claim to the flowers’ size, scent and setting rather than treating preference as a measurement.
evidence: No lily garden in civilization we had ever seen could compare with our lake garden.

questions.prompt: How does the pasque-flower seem to act like a helpful person?
facilitatorNotes: It seems eager to rise and cheer the burned landscape. Readers should separate the observed early flowering from the intention Muir imagines for the plant.
evidence: seemed to be in haste to rise and cheer the desolate landscape.

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: shapes, colours and woodland harvests
days.challenge: Track changing criteria of attention: shape, colour, memory and taste.
days.focus: How the child’s appetite and the adult’s descriptive eye coexist.
days.context: Continue Muir’s description of plants around the family farm, moving from admired flowers to gathered fruits and nuts.
days.contentNote: The historical flower names include “Indian moccasins” and “Turk’s-turban,” retained as Muir’s wording.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, lady’s-slippers through the wild-apple challenge; opens “The next great flower wonders on which we lavished admiration, not only for beauty of color and size”; closes “ed to fill our pockets with them and dare each other to eat one without making a face,—no easy feat.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the lady’s-slippers especially striking to the newcomers?
facilitatorNotes: Their shape differs from familiar Scottish flowers and suggests footwear. Muir shows knowledgeable adults wondering like children, not simply naming plants.
evidence: made them gaze and wonder like children

questions.prompt: How does the hickory paragraph distinguish what interests him as a boy from what he notices as a writer?
facilitatorNotes: He now praises autumn colour, but admits that sweet sap and nuts attracted the boys first. The admission keeps the child’s practical pleasures inside the adult’s lyrical account.
evidence: it was the sweet sap and sweet nuts that first interested us.

questions.prompt: What does the final wild-apple game add after the beautiful descriptions?
facilitatorNotes: The sour apples introduce bodily reaction and playful competition. The ending makes discovery lively and imperfect: not everything found in the woods tastes sweet.
evidence: dare each other to eat one without making a face

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: the changing bird neighbourhood
days.challenge: Separate reported observation from the narrator’s reasonable but uncertain inference.
days.focus: How he makes birds familiar without losing sight of their different habits.
days.context: Muir recalls observing birds around the Wisconsin farm across spring, summer, autumn and winter.
days.contentNote: The passage describes birds defending nests, without graphic injury. “Settlers” identifies the narrator’s viewpoint on the land.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, opening through the brown thrasher; opens “The Wisconsin oak openings were a summer paradise for song birds, and a fine place to get acquainted”; closes “e air fairly quiver. We boys often tried to interpret the wild ringing melody and put it into words.”.

questions.prompt: Why were the oak openings a useful place to watch the whole cycle of bird life?
facilitatorNotes: The widely spaced trees let the boys see arrival, nesting, feeding young and autumn gathering. The answer should connect the physical setting to observation over time.
evidence: the trees stood wide apart

questions.prompt: Which statement about migration goes beyond what the boys actually saw?
facilitatorNotes: They found the birds gone one morning and inferred night migration; Muir explicitly says they never saw the departure. That is a supported inference, not a witnessed event.
evidence: Strange to say, we never saw them start.

questions.prompt: How can the gentle singers also be brave fighters in this passage?
facilitatorNotes: The bluebirds, robins and thrashers defend nests and young. Muir treats fierce behaviour as care for home; readers should name a particular defensive action rather than call the birds simply good or bad.
evidence: birds so gentle could be so bold

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: a chorus and winter music
days.challenge: Interpret sound words and an extended comparison without treating them as literal scientific descriptions.
days.focus: How musical language gives different species distinct characters.
days.context: This separate excerpt compares different bird voices and then turns toward birds that stay through winter.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, redwing blackbirds through the winter owls; opens “One of the gayest of the singers is the redwing blackbird. In the spring, when his scarlet epaulets ”; closes “ooting of the species with the widest throat seemed to us the very wildest of all the winter sounds.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the blackbirds’ gathering resemble a church congregation in Muir’s comparison?
facilitatorNotes: They rise together, settle and burst into concert as a large group. The comparison organizes their coordinated movement and sound; it does not mean the birds follow a human ceremony.
evidence: Let the congregation arise and sing.

questions.prompt: Why can a small song sparrow move Muir more than a huge chorus?
facilitatorNotes: He values richness, sweetness and feeling, not merely volume or numbers. Accept different descriptions of the emotion if tied to the small bird’s song and the boys’ tears.
evidence: The richness, sweetness, and pathos of this small darling’s song

questions.prompt: How does comparing the boys’ feet with the nuthatches’ toes deepen their wonder?
facilitatorNotes: Their own thick socks and boots fail to prevent cold, while the birds seem cheerful with bare toes. The contrast frames a question arising from experience rather than a tested explanation of temperature regulation.
evidence: when our own were so painfully frosted though clad in thick socks and boots.

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: a hunger for books
days.challenge: Follow an argument in which both speakers appeal to the same authority differently.
days.focus: The difference between memorising rules and wanting to understand.
days.context: As a teenager, Muir works on the farm and reads whenever he can. His father welcomes some study but distrusts books outside a strict religious rule.
days.contentNote: The family disagreement turns on Christian belief and strict parental authority in a nineteenth-century household.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, opening argument about learning and spectacles; opens “I learned arithmetic in Scotland without understanding any of it, though I had the rules by heart. B”; closes “ation, and ordered me to return it to the accommodating owner. I managed, however, to read it later.”.

questions.prompt: What changes between Muir’s school arithmetic and his later independent study?
facilitatorNotes: Earlier he knew rules by heart without understanding; later desire and readiness let him use small spare intervals productively. The account does not prove that teachers are unnecessary for everyone.
evidence: without understanding any of it, though I had the rules by heart

questions.prompt: Why does Muir first expect the book called Christian Philosopher to be acceptable, and why is he wrong?
facilitatorNotes: He relies on the title’s first word, but Father focuses on “Philosopher” and a biblical warning. Their attention to different words exposes their disagreement over what kinds of knowledge are safe.
evidence: father balked at the word “Philosopher,”

questions.prompt: How do spectacles challenge Father’s claim that the Bible is the only necessary book?
facilitatorNotes: Muir argues that reading itself may depend on optics and people with scientific knowledge. Father replies that other people can supply it; Muir then challenges whether that reply fits Father’s hope that all will share his faith.
evidence: spectacles cannot be made without some knowledge of the science of optics.

days.title: The boy who moves gently — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Use small movements and sensory details to understand a first impression.
days.focus: Dickon’s introduction shows his character through the responses of animals and Mary.
days.context: After leaving Ben, Mary follows a strange low sound into the wood. Martha’s brother has been asked to bring her gardening supplies.
days.contentNote: Mary’s first impression includes class judgments and a generalizing comparison with snake-charming in India, part of the narrator’s period viewpoint.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Dickon; begins "There was a laurel-hedged walk which curved round the secret garden and ended at a gate which opened"; ends "as poppies will. Them as'll come up an' bloom if you just whistle to 'em, them's th' nicest of all."". Complete source paragraphs 647–665 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Dickon rise so slowly, and what tells us his method works?
facilitatorNotes: He wants not to startle the animals. They leave when he stands, but do not behave as if frightened, so his care affects how the departure feels.
evidence: though not at all as if they were frightened.

questions.prompt: How do smell and color connect Dickon to the surrounding landscape?
facilitatorNotes: Poppy-red cheeks, grass, leaves and heather make him seem at home outdoors. These comparisons support Mary’s sense that he belongs with the creatures, not merely near them.
evidence: almost as if he were made of them.

questions.prompt: What shifts in Mary between asking about the letter and suggesting the log?
facilitatorNotes: She begins stiff and shy, then forgets that shyness and invites him to sit. His easy manner and the shared purpose of examining seeds create a practical beginning to friendship.
evidence: she forgot that she had felt shy.

days.title: Reading a robin’s reply — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish observable animal behavior from Dickon’s playful interpretation of it.
days.focus: Long attention to animals becomes a form of companionship and imagination.
days.context: Mary and Dickon have met and are looking at flower seeds on a log when a robin calls from a holly bush.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Dickon; begins "He stopped and turned his head quickly, his poppy-cheeked face lighting up."; ends "ink p'raps I'm a bird, or a fox, or a rabbit, or a squirrel, or even a beetle, an' I don't know it."". Complete source paragraphs 666–680 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What can Mary actually observe when Dickon appears to speak with the robin?
facilitatorNotes: He approaches slowly, imitates a twitter, and the bird listens and answers. Those are observable actions; the exact human sentences he gives the robin are an interpretation.
evidence: made a sound almost like the robin's own twitter

questions.prompt: What evidence does Dickon give that the bird likes Mary?
facilitatorNotes: He says it would not come near someone it disliked, and points to its approach. His interpretation reassures Mary, whose repeated questions reveal how much that friendship matters.
evidence: He wouldn't come near thee if he didn't

questions.prompt: How does Dickon explain his ability without claiming that he learned a literal bird dictionary?
facilitatorNotes: He describes living nearby and watching the birds from hatching through flight and song. His joking thought that he might be an animal emphasizes identification developed through experience.
evidence: I've watched 'em break shell an' come out an' fledge an' learn to fly an' begin to sing

days.title: “I’ve stolen a garden” — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Notice a character’s pauses, gestures and contradictory words during a difficult confession.
days.focus: The garden means belonging to Mary, making a practical question emotionally charged.
days.context: Dickon has brought seeds and offered gardening advice. Mary has not yet revealed the hidden place where she has been working.
days.contentNote: The narrator describes Mary’s mood as “imperious and Indian,” shorthand for the commanding manner she learned in colonial India.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Dickon; begins "He laughed and came back to the log and began to talk about the flower seeds again. He told her what"; ends ""Eh!" he almost whispered, "it is a queer, pretty place! It's like as if a body was in a dream."". Complete source paragraphs 681–704 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Dickon’s offer to plant the seeds make Mary miserable instead of delighted?
facilitatorNotes: Helping requires knowing where the garden is, which threatens her secret. Her silence and clenched hands show the conflict between wanting a friend and fearing discovery.
evidence: She had never thought of this. She felt miserable.

questions.prompt: How does Dickon demonstrate that he can keep a secret?
facilitatorNotes: He explains that wild animals’ nests and young depend on his silence. That is a relevant history of protecting vulnerable places, not simply a promise without reasons.
evidence: there'd be naught safe on th' moor

questions.prompt: Why does Mary say both that she has stolen the garden and that nobody has a right to take it away?
facilitatorNotes: She knows she lacks permission but feels that discovery and care give her a claim. Discuss the emotional reasoning without requiring agreement that finding property makes it hers.
evidence: Nobody has any right to take it from me when I care about it and they don't.

questions.prompt: When Mary finally shows Dickon the garden, the narrator calls her contrary, obstinate and imperious. Why might she reveal her secret in that mood?
facilitatorNotes: She is afraid of losing the garden, so she shows it as a challenge. Her claim to be the only one who wants it alive mixes possessiveness with care, and Dickon’s pitying look suggests he senses her loneliness.
evidence: Mary stood and waved her hand round defiantly
I'm the only one in the world who wants it to be alive.

days.title: The evidence of living wood — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Follow how an experienced character tests a possibility rather than trusting appearances.
days.focus: The discovery of green wood turns uncertainty into a reasoned hope.
days.context: Mary has just led Dickon through the hidden door, and he has called the garden “a queer, pretty place.” This continues directly at the opening of Chapter XI.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, The Nest of the Missel Thrush; begins "For two or three minutes he stood looking round him, while Mary watched him, and then he began to wa"; ends "up at the climbing and hanging sprays above him--"there'll be a fountain o' roses here this summer."". Complete source paragraphs 707–732 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Dickon first imagine nests rather than a tidy flower display?
facilitatorNotes: He notices secluded tangled branches and a lack of disturbance. His attention follows the needs of birds, revealing what he values in the neglected place.
evidence: It'd be th' safest nestin' place in England.

questions.prompt: What two kinds of evidence help Dickon distinguish live growth from dead wood?
facilitatorNotes: He notices newer brownish-green shoots and examines a cut surface that is greenish and juicy. Dry wood that breaks easily provides a contrasting sign.
evidence: When th' inside is dry an' breaks easy

questions.prompt: How does the image of a fountain of roses change the reader’s picture of the garden?
facilitatorNotes: The image imagines abundant rising and falling flowers where Mary has seen a gray tangle. Its confidence follows actual evidence of living roots and wood rather than appearing as an unexplained promise.
evidence: a fountain o' roses here this summer.

days.title: A garden need not be tidy — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Balance agreement between characters with a new question that their evidence raises.
days.focus: Care can preserve wildness, while signs of past care create a mystery.
days.context: Dickon has shown Mary that some roses still live. They work together around the roots and begin to compare their ideas of what the garden should become.
days.contentNote: Dickon boasts that fresh air keeps him from catching colds, and the children discuss body size.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, The Nest of the Missel Thrush; begins "They went from bush to bush and from tree to tree. He was very strong and clever with his knife and "; ends ""Aye! how could it!" he murmured. "With th' door locked an' th' key buried."". Complete source paragraphs 733–763 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why is Dickon’s praise of Mary’s clearings more than empty encouragement?
facilitatorNotes: He examines the space she made around shoots and identifies the flowers. His approval confirms that her earlier observation led to useful work.
evidence: A gardener couldn't have told thee better.

questions.prompt: What kind of improvement do both children reject?
facilitatorNotes: They do not want everything clipped and perfectly orderly. They want plants alive while keeping the tangles that make the place feel secret; care and tidiness are not identical for them.
evidence: all clipped an' spick an' span

questions.prompt: What detail challenges Mary’s belief that no one has entered the garden for ten years?
facilitatorNotes: Dickon sees signs of more recent pruning. The locked door and buried key remain contrary evidence, so the scene ends with a real puzzle rather than a solution.
evidence: a bit o' prunin' done here an' there, later than ten year' ago.

days.title: A teasing rhyme becomes a plan — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Connect an embedded rhyme with a change in the meaning of a repeated label.
days.focus: Friendship allows Mary to reclaim an image previously used to hurt her.
days.context: While working with Dickon, Mary remembers the garden rhyme other children used to tease her. Here the rhyme leads to a different conversation.
days.contentNote: The narrator briefly generalizes about people in India while describing language learning.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, The Nest of the Missel Thrush; begins "Mistress Mary always felt that however many years she lived she should never forget that first morni"; ends ""That's two, then," said Mary. "That's two for me."". Complete source paragraphs 764–787 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary suddenly ask about flowers shaped like bells?
facilitatorNotes: The teasing rhyme includes silver bells, and the real garden gives her a way to imagine them as actual flowers. A hurtful memory becomes a practical planting idea.
evidence: it made me wonder if there were really flowers like silver bells.

questions.prompt: How does Dickon respond to Mary’s lingering anger at the children who teased her?
facilitatorNotes: He points to flowers, wild creatures and their homes rather than arguing over who was more contrary. Mary stops frowning, showing the response redirects her attention.
evidence: there doesn't seem to be no need for no one to be contrary

questions.prompt: What is important about Mary asking “Does tha’ like me?” in Dickon’s speech?
facilitatorNotes: She risks asking for friendship directly and tries to meet him in his familiar language. His warm answer turns her count of people she likes into evidence that she is liked too.
evidence: That's two for me.

days.title: As safe as a nest — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Interpret an extended comparison using the character’s earlier actions in this excerpt.
days.focus: Dickon’s ordinary meal and promise make a seemingly magical friendship dependable.
days.context: Mary and Dickon have spent their first morning working together in the hidden garden. The dinner bell means she must leave.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, The Nest of the Missel Thrush; begins "And then they began to work harder than ever and more joyfully. Mary was startled and sorry when she"; ends "And she was quite sure she was.". Complete source paragraphs 788–802 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does Dickon’s packed dinner affect what each child can do next?
facilitatorNotes: Mary must return to the house, while his bread and bacon let him stay and keep working. The ordinary practical detail explains their separation without breaking his commitment to the garden.
evidence: My dinner's easy to carry about with me

questions.prompt: Why does Mary imagine Dickon might be a wood fairy?
facilitatorNotes: He seems almost impossibly suited to the garden, and she fears he could vanish. The image describes her delighted uncertainty about a new friend, not proof that he is supernatural.
evidence: He seemed too good to be true.

questions.prompt: Why is the missel-thrush comparison a fitting answer to her question about secrecy?
facilitatorNotes: Dickon treats her secret as a vulnerable nest he would protect. The assurance draws on his care for wild creatures and gives Mary a way to understand trust.
evidence: Tha' art as safe as a missel thrush.

days.title: Different ideas of beauty — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Compare two characters’ descriptions without assuming one must be literally incorrect.
days.focus: Admiration changes which features Mary values and how she describes a friend.
days.context: Mary returns indoors after meeting Dickon. Martha asks about her brother and the gardening supplies he brought.
days.contentNote: The characters discuss conventional ideas of facial beauty.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, Might I Have a Bit of Earth?; begins "Mary ran so fast that she was rather out of breath when she reached her room. Her hair was ruffled o"; ends ""There wouldn't be no reason," answered Martha. "You wouldn't do no harm."". Complete source paragraphs 805–829 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Martha seem both pleased and doubtful when Mary calls Dickon beautiful?
facilitatorNotes: Martha loves him but has not thought of his turned-up nose or round eyes as handsome. Her affection and conventional judgment of appearance pull in different directions.
evidence: she looked pleased, too.

questions.prompt: How does Mary defend the features Martha questions?
facilitatorNotes: She says she likes the turned-up nose and round eyes and compares their color to the moor sky. Her response links beauty to affection and the natural world.
evidence: exactly the color of the sky over the moor.

questions.prompt: Why does a discussion of where to plant flowers make Mary anxious?
facilitatorNotes: Martha believes she still needs an approved plot, while Mary already gardens secretly. Mary asks about an unwanted place to seek reassurance without revealing it.
evidence: If it was out of the way and no one wanted it

days.title: A guardian tries to listen — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Infer discomfort from gestures and short dialogue on both sides of a conversation.
days.focus: Fear begins to change when two people acknowledge what they do not know.
days.context: Mary has been summoned to meet her uncle and guardian, Mr. Craven, who has been grieving and absent. She fears that the meeting will end her freedom to garden.
days.contentNote: The narration uses a demeaning period term for spinal difference when describing Mr. Craven.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, Might I Have a Bit of Earth?; begins "She was taken to a part of the house she had not been into before. At last Mrs. Medlock knocked at a"; ends " Her daughter had talked about you. She thought you needed fresh air and freedom and running about."". Complete source paragraphs 843–880 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What suggests that Mr. Craven is distracted rather than simply uninterested in Mary’s answers?
facilitatorNotes: He rubs his forehead, seems to see something beyond her, and admits forgetting arrangements for her. These details show distress and inattention, although they do not excuse the neglect.
evidence: as if they were seeing something else

questions.prompt: How does mentioning Mrs. Sowerby help Mary make her request?
facilitatorNotes: It gives both people a shared trusted person. Mary emphasizes her experience with twelve children, and Mr. Craven remembers that she advised outdoor play.
evidence: She knows about children

questions.prompt: What changes when Mr. Craven calls himself a poor guardian?
facilitatorNotes: He acknowledges limits and explains his wish that Mary be happy, while admitting he cannot provide enough time or attention. Mary’s fear meets a more complicated person than she expected.
evidence: I am your guardian, though I am a poor one for any child.

days.title: Permission and a small promise — The Secret Garden excerpt
days.challenge: Connect a request, an indirect memory and a written message across changes of setting.
days.focus: A little patch of earth and a brief note offer two different kinds of reassurance.
days.context: Mr. Craven has listened to advice that Mary needs room to play outdoors. He asks whether she wants something before he leaves again.
days.contentNote: Adults express period beliefs about health and education.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, Might I Have a Bit of Earth?; begins ""She knows all about children," Mary said again in spite of herself."; ends ""I will cum bak."". Complete source paragraphs 881–907 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary’s request for earth surprise Mr. Craven?
facilitatorNotes: He offers familiar possessions such as toys and books, but she wants a place to grow living things. Her request reveals a changed interest that material gifts alone would not satisfy.
evidence: might I have a bit of earth?

questions.prompt: What suggests that the request reaches a memory important to him?
facilitatorNotes: He covers his eyes, repeats the words, and becomes softer before mentioning someone else who loved growing things. The excerpt hints at grief without giving a full explanation.
evidence: You remind me of some one else who loved the earth and things that grow.

questions.prompt: Why does Dickon’s short note matter even though he is not there?
facilitatorNotes: Mary fears he may have disappeared like a fairy, but the reused paper and nest drawing are tangible signs that he intends to return. The short, imperfect spelling communicates a dependable promise.
evidence: I will cum bak.

days.title: January (A Calendar of Sonnets)
days.challenge: Follow a turn from landscape description to direct advice.
days.focus: A paradox of cold surroundings and inner strength.
days.context: Jackson addresses winter and then a human heart. Read the complete sonnet twice; the second reading should test whether the apparent stillness means death or preparation.

excerpt.locator:
January (A Calendar of Sonnets); source text begins "O winter! frozen pulse and heart of fire,
  What loss is theirs who from thy kingdom turn
  Dis" and ends "ent rose.
  Walk boldly on the white untrodden snows,
  The winter is the winter's own release.".

questions.prompt: What makes frozen pulse and heart of fire an apparent contradiction?
facilitatorNotes: Frozen suggests inactivity while fire suggests energy. Later sleeping roses and flowing streams develop the possibility of hidden life.
evidence: frozen pulse and heart of fire

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker imagine June hiring its roses?
facilitatorNotes: The personification gives June a tempting offer which the roses would refuse: winter rest teaches strength. This is a poetic explanation, not a botanical experiment.
evidence: the strength they learn

questions.prompt: Where does the address shift, and what does winter now represent?
facilitatorNotes: O Heart introduces emotional advice. Winter becomes an image for quieter or difficult periods in which inward warmth and rest remain possible.
evidence: Keep warm by inner fires

days.title: February (A Calendar of Sonnets)
days.challenge: Unpack a long sentence and repeated phrases of judgment.
days.focus: Stillness as an opportunity to reconsider past actions.
days.context: Expiation means making amends for wrongs. Jackson associates a quiet winter month with reflection before spring activity; this is a poetic argument about how to use time.

questions.prompt: Which details keep the opening from describing a wholly motionless world?
facilitatorNotes: Catkins fill and willow stems brighten even while the snow remains. These small changes complicate the claim of no sign of spring.
evidence: willow stems grow daily red and bright

questions.prompt: How do haste and greed change the usual cheerful picture of summer?
facilitatorNotes: They suggest that eagerly seeking pleasure can crowd out reflection. The poem does not condemn every summer joy; it argues for a pause before it.
evidence: dreaming thoughts grow heavy with a greed

questions.prompt: Why repeat “Fit days” near the end?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition insists that this season is particularly suitable for reckoning with losses and future needs; a reader can judge whether the natural description supports that claim.
evidence: To reckon clear the new life's sterner need

days.title: March (A Calendar of Sonnets)
days.challenge: Distinguish violent sound from the speaker’s interpretation of its purpose.
days.focus: An argument made through competing personifications of spring.
days.context: March is associated with Mars, the Roman god of war. Annunciation lilies bring a Christian reference into the closing image. Jackson disputes the war association through her imagined natural scene.

excerpt.locator:
March (A Calendar of Sonnets); source text begins "Month which the warring ancients strangely styled
  The month of war,--as if in their fierce wa" and ends "r the spring;
  And hidden, sacred, in her breast doth bear
  Annunciation lilies for the year.".

questions.prompt: Why does the aside about the ancients challenge the month’s name?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker suggests their habitual warfare tells us more about them than about March. The aside is a sharp judgment in the speaker’s voice.
evidence: Were any month of peace!

questions.prompt: How do the violets answer the clashing wind?
facilitatorNotes: They sleep without fear, like a child. Their response makes the noise seem part of growth rather than a battle threatening all life.
evidence: sleep through all the din, as sleeps a child

questions.prompt: What changes when earth becomes an expectant mother?
facilitatorNotes: The final image replaces destruction with preparation for birth. Hidden lilies support the idea of life not yet visible.
evidence: makes ready for the spring

days.title: The Railway Children: making a supper from scraps
days.challenge: Notice how light, objects and practical actions change the same room’s atmosphere.
days.focus: How an emergency revises the children’s judgment of Aunt Emma.
days.context: The family has reached a dark house and cannot find the expected supper. Mother tries to make an adventure of it.
days.contentNote: A child’s small burn prompts a brief, non-graphic comparison with Roman martyrs. The passage also mentions diluted ginger wine as a historical household drink.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, opening through the two-o’clock chime; opens ““WHAT fun!” said Mother, in the dark, feeling for the matches on the table. “How frightened the poor”; closes “ock ever so far away, she always thought. And she heard, too, Mother still moving about in her room.”.

questions.prompt: How does the room change without the family replacing its furniture?
facilitatorNotes: Candles and a fire reveal carved wood, while tidying and setting the table make it welcoming. The improvement depends partly on seeing familiar objects differently.
evidence: The fire-light and the candle-light made the dining room look very different

questions.prompt: Why is the cupboard food a “real feast” even though it is an odd assortment?
facilitatorNotes: They are hungry, tired and had expected no supper; their effort gives the modest mixture special value. Readers may notice how lists and contrasts make this a feast of relief.
evidence: a real feast was laid out on it.

questions.prompt: What evidence makes the children reconsider Aunt Emma?
facilitatorNotes: Her packed food rescues supper and her aired sheets help them sleep. Affectionate manner and practical thoughtfulness are not identical, so the story complicates their earlier dislike.
evidence: it was she who had thought of packing up the odds and ends of things to eat.

days.title: The Railway Children: helpful intentions and unexpected breakfast
days.challenge: Revise first impressions when later evidence explains a mistake.
days.focus: Good intentions, incomplete knowledge and fairer judgments.
days.context: The children rise early to help in the unfamiliar house and then explore outside.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, the first morning through “To the railway”; opens “Next morning Roberta woke Phyllis by pulling her hair gently, but quite enough for her purpose.”; closes “A. To the railway.”.

questions.prompt: What does the burned kettle show about the children’s attempt to help?
facilitatorNotes: They successfully start the fire but leave too early and too long. The failure comes from missing experience and follow-through, not from wanting to harm anything.
evidence: the water had all boiled away, and the bottom was burned out of the kettle.

questions.prompt: Which new evidence changes the accusation against Mrs. Viney?
facilitatorNotes: The family discovers the fully prepared supper in a room mistaken for a cupboard, plus a note about her son-in-law’s injury. The earlier accusation was based on not finding the food, not proof she had stolen money.
evidence: the supper we ought to have had last night

questions.prompt: How does the little question-and-answer ending convey the children’s agreement?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator turns their shared look into the same silent question and reply. It makes their wish to visit the railway seem immediate and unanimous without requiring three speeches.
evidence: Q. Where shall we go?

days.title: The Railway Children: seeing a whole train
days.challenge: Compare several viewpoints on one familiar machine and notice a hint about later events.
days.focus: How changing position makes the railway seem new.
days.context: After helping unpack, the children visit the nearby railway as observers rather than passengers.
days.contentNote: The children enter railway property and walk beside the tracks.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, the descent to the railway through the porter’s warning; opens “So to the railway they went, and as soon as they started for the railway they saw where the garden h”; closes “riendly sort, with no nonsense about him. But later the words came back to Peter with a new meaning.”.

questions.prompt: Why do Bobbie and Phyllis compare the train and tunnel with a dragon and its lair?
facilitatorNotes: The train shrieks, snorts and rushes from a dark opening; its heat and movement suggest wings. The comparison connects several sensations, not only the train’s size.
evidence: it was like a great dragon tearing by.

questions.prompt: What does Phyllis mean by saying they have seen trains “cut in half”?
facilitatorNotes: Platforms previously hid the lower parts, and the children watched as passengers. From the fence they see the full height; the train itself has not grown.
evidence: We've always seen them cut in half by platforms

questions.prompt: Why does the final sentence make the porter’s joke seem worth remembering?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says the warning will gain a new meaning for Peter. Readers can predict a coal-related problem while recognising that this excerpt does not yet tell what he will do.
evidence: later the words came back to Peter with a new meaning.

days.title: The Railway Children: when “poor” becomes real
days.challenge: Follow an extended comparison and distinguish a persuasive label from a justified action.
days.focus: How Peter builds a heroic story around a plan he suspects may be wrong.
days.context: The countryside has made the children’s new life enjoyable, but a cold spell reveals limits on household money.
days.contentNote: The siblings use make-believe bandit language and a joking threat.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, the rising-dough comparison through the call for the Roman Chariot; opens “Have you ever gone into a farm-house kitchen on a baking day, and seen the great crock of dough set ”; closes ““Come hither with me,” he said, “and bring the Roman Chariot.””.

questions.prompt: What does the dent in rising dough explain about the children’s sorrow, and what does it not mean?
facilitatorNotes: Their pain gradually becomes less visible as new interests fill their lives. The next paragraph says they have not forgotten Father, so the comparison need not mean they no longer care.
evidence: though they did not forget him

questions.prompt: Which ordinary choices finally give the word “poor” a concrete meaning?
facilitatorNotes: They cannot have a coal fire on a cold day or both jam and butter. The restrictions make money’s effect tangible after food and clothing had seemed unchanged.
evidence: Jam or butter, dear—not jam and butter.

questions.prompt: How does Peter make secrecy sound noble even while revealing doubt?
facilitatorNotes: He claims he is protecting his sisters and calls the venture a forlorn hope, but admits it may be wrong and asks for a misleading answer to Mother. Discuss the gap between brave-sounding language and the actual reason for secrecy.
evidence: because it may be wrong, and I don't want to drag you into it.

days.title: The Railway Children: a coal-mine or a theft?
days.challenge: Weigh motivation, evidence and self-justification rather than accepting a character’s preferred label.
days.focus: A forgiving response that still names the wrongdoing.
days.context: Peter leads his sisters to coal he has hidden near the station. Their “Roman Chariot” is an old pram used to carry things. One intervening descriptive paragraph is outside this excerpt; this is a new passage, not an uninterrupted continuation of the previous selection.
days.contentNote: Includes taking coal, the fear of police involvement and an adult grabbing a child’s collar.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Follow your dauntless leader” through chapter end; opens ““Follow your dauntless leader,” said Peter, and led the way down the hill towards the station.”; closes “quite sure. And they were also quite sure that he was quite sure, however little he cared to own it.”.

questions.prompt: What shows that the girls understand more about Peter’s “mine” than he thinks?
facilitatorNotes: They admit knowing the source all along and pretending ignorance to humour him. Their later willingness to share blame challenges his picture of himself as the only informed leader.
evidence: We knew all the time.

questions.prompt: Why does taking coal from the middle of the heap not answer the Station Master’s objection?
facilitatorNotes: The issue is ownership, not how long the outside coal might last. Peter turns a location within a stored pile into a supposed mine, but the whole pile belongs to someone else.
evidence: what's mine isn't yours

questions.prompt: How does the narrator complicate Peter’s final claim that mining may not be a crime?
facilitatorNotes: Peter voices doubt, but the narrator says the girls know he understands. The ending distinguishes what he will admit aloud from what he knows privately.
evidence: I'm not at all sure, even now, that mining is a crime.

days.title: Four wishes and one dollar each — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Compare speakers whose complaints reveal different daily responsibilities.
days.focus: A family disagreement reveals both dissatisfaction and affection.
days.context: The four March sisters talk at home during the American Civil War. Their father is away, and their mother has suggested a Christmas without presents.
days.contentNote: The story is set during the American Civil War. The sisters’ work and school expectations reflect their historical setting.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Playing Pilgrims; begins ""Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents," grumbled Jo, lying on the rug."; ends " though we do have to work, we make fun for ourselves, and are a pretty jolly set, as Jo would say."". Complete source paragraphs 277–297 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does Beth answer the opening complaints, and why does the comfort last only briefly?
facilitatorNotes: She names the family members they still have. Jo then remembers that their father is absent, turning a comforting list into a reminder of separation.
evidence: We've got father and mother and each other

questions.prompt: How does Jo justify spending her dollar on herself?
facilitatorNotes: She argues that a small amount cannot help the army much, that the sisters earned their money, and that hard work deserves a little pleasure. Readers can assess these reasons without assuming wanting a book is itself wrong.
evidence: we work hard enough to earn it

questions.prompt: What does Beth’s comparison with the King children add to the discussion of money?
facilitatorNotes: She observes that wealth does not prevent quarreling. Meg agrees that the sisters have fun despite poverty, complicating the idea that money alone produces happiness.
evidence: we make fun for ourselves

days.title: What kind of girl? — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Compare character judgments with the narrator’s later description.
days.focus: Labels can reveal the speaker’s expectations as much as the person described.
days.context: The sisters’ conversation turns from money to manners. Jo and Amy disagree about how a girl should behave.
days.contentNote: Characters express nineteenth-century gender expectations and judgments about appearance.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Playing Pilgrims; begins ""Jo does use such slang words!" observed Amy, with a reproving look at the long figure stretched on "; ends " mindful of her manners. What the characters of the four sisters were we will leave to be found out.". Complete source paragraphs 298–311 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does Beth interrupt Jo and Amy’s argument without lecturing either sister?
facilitatorNotes: She sings a familiar reminder about birds agreeing in their nests. Its humor changes their mood and shows her role as a peacemaker.
evidence: both sharp voices softened to a laugh

questions.prompt: Why does Jo resist Meg’s advice to remember that she is becoming a young lady?
facilitatorNotes: Jo associates growing up with unwanted clothes, constrained behavior and exclusion from the fighting where her father is. Her objection is to restricted possibilities, not simply to her birthday.
evidence: I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy

questions.prompt: What does the narrator’s description of the room suggest about the family’s resources and priorities?
facilitatorNotes: The carpet is faded and the furniture plain, but books, flowers and pictures make the room comfortable. Modest possessions coexist with pleasure in beauty and learning.
evidence: a comfortable old room

days.title: A different plan for their dollars — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Track a change of plan through several short contributions to a conversation.
days.focus: A shared gift plan grows out of noticing another person’s needs.
days.context: The sisters hear the clock and prepare for their mother’s return. Her worn slippers attract their attention.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Playing Pilgrims; begins "The clock struck six; and, having swept up the hearth, Beth put a pair of slippers down to warm. Som"; ends "stmas night," said Jo, marching up and down, with her hands behind her back and her nose in the air.". Complete source paragraphs 312–329 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why do the slippers change the subject from the sisters’ own wishes?
facilitatorNotes: Their worn condition makes their mother’s need visible. Several sisters immediately volunteer to buy replacements, redirecting money they had planned to spend on themselves.
evidence: They are quite worn out

questions.prompt: How does Beth solve the competition over who will buy the new slippers?
facilitatorNotes: She suggests that everyone buy something for their mother and nothing for themselves. The solution includes each sister and leads to a coordinated list of different gifts.
evidence: each get her something for Christmas

questions.prompt: Why is Beth’s birthday chair described as a trial rather than a treat?
facilitatorNotes: She likes gifts and affection but dislikes being watched while opening packages. The detail distinguishes enjoying love from enjoying attention.
evidence: it was dreadful to have you sit looking at me

days.title: A rehearsal interrupted — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Follow comic contrasts between what performers intend and what actually happens.
days.focus: An imperfect family performance reveals affection and imagination.
days.context: The sisters plan a holiday play. Jo directs, Amy practices a dramatic fall, and Meg worries they are getting too old for acting.
days.contentNote: The children rehearse a melodramatic play with pretend danger and references to stage deaths; no one is harmed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Playing Pilgrims; begins ""I don't mean to act any more after this time; I'm getting too old for such things," observed Meg, w"; ends "d kitchen, quiet and busy; while Amy gave directions to every one, as she sat with her hands folded.". Complete source paragraphs 330–344 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does Jo persuade Meg to remain in the play?
facilitatorNotes: She appeals to Meg’s acting ability and a handsome costume, promising that it can be the last such performance. The argument combines praise with a compromise.
evidence: You are the best actress

questions.prompt: Why is Amy’s attempted faint funny in comparison with Jo’s demonstration?
facilitatorNotes: Jo throws herself into a theatrical collapse, while Amy moves stiffly and cries out as if pricked. The narrator sets an ideal dramatic gesture against an awkward rehearsal.
evidence: more suggestive of pins being run into her

questions.prompt: What changes when their mother enters?
facilitatorNotes: The activity becomes a practical welcome: each child helps with clothing, warmth or comfort. The shift from theatrical roles to familiar tasks shows another way the sisters act together.
evidence: The girls flew about

days.title: A letter and four responses — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Compare an absent character’s message with the listeners’ different reactions.
days.focus: An appeal to courage becomes a challenge for ordinary life at home.
days.context: Mrs. March has a letter from the girls’ father, who is serving as a chaplain during the Civil War. The family gathers to hear it.
days.contentNote: The family discusses wartime absence and Christian ideas of duty. These are the characters’ historical circumstances and beliefs.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Playing Pilgrims; begins "As they gathered about the table, Mrs. March said, with a particularly happy face, "I've got a treat"; ends "ttle soul to be all that father hoped to find her when the year brought round the happy coming home.". Complete source paragraphs 345–362 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator describe what Father leaves out of his letter?
facilitatorNotes: He says little about hardship and danger and dwells on affection and hope. This choice suggests that he wants to reassure his family, though it does not mean his work is easy.
evidence: In this one little was said of the hardships endured

questions.prompt: What does Father mean by the battles the girls can fight at home?
facilitatorNotes: He asks them to overcome selfish habits and support their mother. The language turns moral effort into a parallel to wartime courage.
evidence: fight their bosom enemies bravely

questions.prompt: How is Beth’s response different from the promises made by her sisters?
facilitatorNotes: She says nothing, wipes away tears and resumes knitting. The quiet action matches the narrator’s emphasis on her existing effort to do her duty.
evidence: Beth said nothing

days.title: Playing pilgrims in daily life — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Follow an extended metaphor from a childhood game into daily responsibilities.
days.focus: Imagining work as a journey helps the family talk about real difficulties.
days.context: After hearing their father’s letter, the girls remember a game based on Pilgrim’s Progress, a Christian allegory of a difficult journey toward goodness.
days.contentNote: The passage draws on the Christian allegory of Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress and a guidebook associated with the family’s faith.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Playing Pilgrims; begins "Mrs. March broke the silence that followed Jo's words, by saying in her cheery voice, "Do you rememb"; ends "ound at night was the same cheery sound, for the girls never grew too old for that familiar lullaby.". Complete source paragraphs 364–381 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What makes the remembered roof seem like the end of an important journey?
facilitatorNotes: Beth remembers sunshine, pleasant things, rest and happiness. These sensory rewards give the game’s destination emotional meaning.
evidence: all stood and sung for joy

questions.prompt: Why does Mother say they can still play pilgrims even though they are older?
facilitatorNotes: She connects the game’s burdens and road with real worries and the effort to improve. The game becomes a metaphor rather than an instruction to repeat a childish performance.
evidence: Our burdens are here

questions.prompt: How do the sisters make their sewing task resemble an adventure?
facilitatorNotes: They divide the long seams into continents and talk about the countries as they stitch. The imagined journey makes repetitive work shared and interesting.
evidence: dividing the long seams into four parts

days.title: Christmas books and a larger bottle — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Notice how a good intention can coexist with a lingering desire for praise.
days.focus: Amy’s changed gift shows real effort without making her suddenly perfect.
days.context: On Christmas morning each sister finds a small book from their mother. They also finish arranging the gifts they bought for her.
days.contentNote: The family reads a Christian devotional gift. The activity and values belong to this family’s historical setting.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, A Merry Christmas; begins "Jo was the first to wake in the gray dawn of Christmas morning. No stockings hung at the fireplace, "; ends "d the corner and changed it the minute I was up: and I'm _so_ glad, for mine is the handsomest now."". Complete source paragraphs 386–405 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does the shared reading make the four different gifts into a common activity?
facilitatorNotes: The books have individual colors, but the older sisters help the younger ones with difficult words and passages. Reading becomes mutual support rather than four isolated tasks.
evidence: I'll help you with the hard words

questions.prompt: Why has Amy gone out early to exchange her bottle of cologne?
facilitatorNotes: She regrets keeping money for herself and buys a larger bottle using all she has. The action corrects an earlier compromise between generosity and her own wishes.
evidence: I gave _all_ my money to get it

questions.prompt: What does Amy’s remark about having the handsomest gift reveal after her generous decision?
facilitatorNotes: She has made an effort to be less selfish but still enjoys comparison and admiration. The narrator lets progress and vanity exist together.
evidence: mine is the handsomest now

days.title: A breakfast given away — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Track the cost of generosity as well as the satisfaction characters feel afterward.
days.focus: Giving becomes concrete when the girls carry food and help in the room.
days.context: The March family is about to eat a special Christmas breakfast when their mother describes a nearby family with a new baby and very little food or warmth.
days.contentNote: This scene depicts poverty, hunger and a sick mother without graphic detail. The narrator renders the German immigrant family’s English in a patronizing way typical of the period.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, A Merry Christmas; begins "Another bang of the street-door sent the basket under the sofa, and the girls to the table, eager fo"; ends "e-festivals so pleasant at the time, so sweet to remember long afterward, and then all fell to work.". Complete source paragraphs 406–428 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does the minute of silence matter before Jo answers her mother?
facilitatorNotes: The girls are hungry and have been waiting for breakfast. The pause acknowledges a real sacrifice before their willing agreement.
evidence: for a minute no one spoke

questions.prompt: Which actions show that the visit provides more than food?
facilitatorNotes: Hannah makes a fire and covers broken panes, their mother cares for the baby, and the girls serve the children. Several practical needs are met together.
evidence: stopped up the broken panes with old hats

questions.prompt: How can the narrator call this a merry breakfast when the sisters do not eat it?
facilitatorNotes: They enjoy helping and watching others eat. Their happiness comes from the shared event rather than the meal they originally expected.
evidence: though they didn't get any of it

days.title: A snowball begins a visit — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish what Jo observes from what she assumes about another household.
days.focus: Initiative turns distant sympathy into a chance for friendship.
days.context: Jo has met Laurie at a party but has not yet visited his grand house next door. A snowy afternoon gives her an idea.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, Being Neighborly; begins ""What in the world are you going to do now, Jo?" asked Meg, one snowy afternoon, as her sister came "; ends ", asking for "Mr. Laurie," and a surprised-looking servant came running up to announce a young lady.". Complete source paragraphs 683–710 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: What makes the wealthy house seem less inviting than the shabby March house?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator describes luxurious objects alongside a lack of children, visitors and a welcoming face. Material comfort contrasts with a lonely atmosphere.
evidence: a lonely, lifeless sort of house

questions.prompt: Which parts of Jo’s explanation for Laurie’s loneliness does their conversation confirm?
facilitatorNotes: He has been shut up for a week with a cold and lacks company he wants. Her claim that his grandfather knows nothing about his needs is an assumption, not something Laurie confirms here.
evidence: been shut up a week

questions.prompt: How does the invitation emerge from Jo’s questions rather than a direct demand to visit?
facilitatorNotes: She asks about reading and company, then reminds him that he knows her family. He invites her, and she goes to ask permission. The exchange lets him express a wish.
evidence: Will you come, please?

days.title: Comfort that cannot be bought — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Infer emotional needs from a character’s description of an ordinary window.
days.focus: Reciprocal kindness begins when Jo recognizes a kind of wealth she already has.
days.context: Jo arrives to visit Laurie, who is recovering from a cold. Each of her sisters has contributed something to the visit.
days.contentNote: Laurie mentions that his mother has died. A character also blames servants for an untidy room.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, Being Neighborly; begins ""All right, show her up, it's Miss Jo," said Laurie, going to the door of his little parlor to meet "; ends "much good-will in Jo, it was impossible not to take her blunt speeches as kindly as they were meant.".
