days.context: Beth has permission to practice at the Laurences’ piano without an audience. Her gratitude leads her to plan a handmade present.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, Beth Finds the Palace Beautiful; begins "Beth had a rapture with her mother, and then rushed up to impart the glorious news to her family of "; ends "el so queer! Oh, it is too lovely!" and Beth hid her face in Jo's apron, quite upset by her present.". Complete source paragraphs 838–851 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why is the music lying on the piano unlikely to be there by pure accident?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator’s playful phrase is followed by details of music supplied for Beth and people protecting her practice time. Readers can infer a deliberate welcome that she does not notice.
evidence: for her especial benefit

questions.prompt: How does the slipper project make Beth’s thanks a family effort?
facilitatorNotes: Her mother pays for finishing, sisters help choose materials and handle hard parts, and Laurie delivers the gift secretly. Beth’s own work is supported by several people.
evidence: with occasional lifts over hard parts

questions.prompt: How does the delay before an acknowledgment create a contrast with what happens next?
facilitatorNotes: Beth fears she offended him, but the family’s excitement and the piano reveal the opposite. Her uncertainty magnifies the surprise.
evidence: beginning to fear she had offended

days.title: Gratitude overcomes a fear — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Compare the meaning of an expensive object with the personal history attached to it.
days.focus: Understanding another person’s loss changes Beth’s ability to approach him.
days.context: Beth has found a small piano sent to her by Mr. Laurence. Her sisters help her read his accompanying letter.
days.contentNote: The passage gently discusses the death of a child and a grieving grandparent. Affectionate physical contact is portrayed as welcome within this friendship.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, Beth Finds the Palace Beautiful; begins "Jo opened the paper, and began to laugh, for the first words she saw were,--"; ends "urprise; and Meg exclaimed, with uplifted hands, "Well, I do believe the world is coming to an end!"". Complete source paragraphs 852–870 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why is the piano more personal than a newly purchased reward?
facilitatorNotes: It belonged to the granddaughter Mr. Laurence lost and whose things he carefully kept. Sending it connects his grief with affection for Beth.
evidence: something which once belonged to the little granddaughter he lost

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator say the piano’s real charm lies in Beth’s face?
facilitatorNotes: The instrument is attractive and well tuned, but the joy it gives her is what matters most in the description. Its value becomes visible through her response.
evidence: the real charm of it lay in the happiest of all happy faces

questions.prompt: What allows Beth to finish her visit even though she cannot finish her thank-you speech?
facilitatorNotes: She notices his friendliness and remembers his lost granddaughter, then expresses affection directly. Concern for him displaces her attention to her own fear.
evidence: only remembering that he had lost the little girl he loved

days.title: A week without work — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Compare confident predictions with the small disappointments already appearing.
days.focus: An experiment begins to reveal what the characters take for granted.
days.context: Summer vacation begins. The sisters propose giving up lessons and household work for a week, and their mother lets them test the plan.
days.contentNote: The passage describes the household roles of a nineteenth-century family.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, Experiments; begins ""The first of June! The Kings are off to the seashore to-morrow, and I'm free. Three months' vacatio"; ends "o examined her work with interest, she went to walk, got caught in a shower, and came home dripping.". Complete source paragraphs 1292–1308 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How do Meg’s and Jo’s plans reveal different ideas of rest?
facilitatorNotes: Meg wants late mornings and doing nothing; Jo wants books, outdoor reading and lively fun with Laurie. Both want freedom from obligations but imagine different pleasures.
evidence: I shall lie abed late, and do nothing

questions.prompt: What does Mother predict, and how does she make room for the girls to test it?
facilitatorNotes: She predicts that all play can be as bad as all work but gives them a week. Her response allows experience rather than immediate prohibition to test the idea.
evidence: You may try your experiment for a week

questions.prompt: Which details of the first morning suggest that rest depends on work someone usually does?
facilitatorNotes: Meg finds a lonely breakfast, empty vases, dust and scattered books. The neglected jobs affect the setting in which she hoped to relax.
evidence: Nothing was neat and pleasant but

days.title: The hidden work becomes visible — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish what characters admit aloud from what narration reveals about their experience.
days.focus: A change in routine exposes the labor behind everyday comfort.
days.context: The March sisters are testing a week devoted entirely to enjoyment. Their mother and Hannah have quietly kept the household running.
days.contentNote: Historical class and gender expectations shape the narration. The word ennui means boredom or weary dissatisfaction.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, Experiments; begins "At tea-time they compared notes, and all agreed that it had been a delightful, though unusually long"; ends "o that their feelings might not be hurt,--a motherly little deception, for which they were grateful.". Complete source paragraphs 1310–1320 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why is the claim that the experiment is working finely doubtful?
facilitatorNotes: The narration lists boredom, irritability, damaged clothes and disappointment. The girls insist on success despite evidence that each is dissatisfied.
evidence: they assured their mother that the experiment was working finely

questions.prompt: What makes Saturday different from the earlier days of the experiment?
facilitatorNotes: Their mother gives Hannah a holiday and stays in her room. The girls experience the effect of their neglected work without others quietly doing it for them.
evidence: let the girls enjoy the full effect of the play system

questions.prompt: How does the breakfast show that willingness alone does not guarantee skill?
facilitatorNotes: The girls begin eagerly but boil bitter tea, scorch the omelette and spoil biscuits. Their mother kindly accepts the tray while having arranged other food for herself.
evidence: Housekeeping ain't no joke

days.title: Pip and a rash invitation — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Notice how comic overconfidence and real grief share one scene.
days.focus: The experiment’s first serious consequence falls on the most helpless member of the household.
days.context: It is the last day of the sisters’ week without regular work. Mother has given Hannah, the family’s servant, a holiday and said she would stay in her room and take care of herself; the girls sent a breakfast tray up anyway, and it was spoiled. Meg, acting as cook, is upset by her failures.
days.contentNote: Beth’s canary, Pip, has died of hunger because she forgot to feed him; the sisters plan his funeral.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, Experiments; begins "Many were the complaints below, and great the chagrin of the head cook at her failures. "Never mind,"; ends " we'll have a nice little funeral," said Jo, beginning to feel as if she had undertaken a good deal.". Complete source paragraphs 1321–1338 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why do Meg and Mother each refuse to help with Jo’s dinner, and what does each refusal show?
facilitatorNotes: Meg objects that Jo invited Laurie on her own responsibility; Mother announces a holiday of her own. Readers may suspect Mother’s holiday is deliberate, since it leaves the girls to meet the consequences of the experiment.
evidence: I wash my hands of the dinner-party
I'm going to take a vacation to-day

questions.prompt: What comparison shows how strange Mother’s idle morning seems to Jo, and why is it funny?
facilitatorNotes: Jo treats her mother rocking and reading as if it were a natural disaster. The exaggeration is comic, but it also shows how constantly Mother usually works.
evidence: an eclipse, an earthquake, or a volcanic eruption would hardly have seemed stranger

questions.prompt: How does the description of Pip make his death a result of the experiment rather than a simple accident?
facilitatorNotes: The claws seem to beg for food, Beth says there is no seed left, and Jo says Pip has had the worst of the experiment. A neglected daily duty has a consequence that cannot be undone.
evidence: as if imploring the food for want of which he had died
Pip has had the worst of the experiment

questions.prompt: Compare Beth’s, Amy’s and Jo’s responses to Pip’s death. What does each reveal?
facilitatorNotes: Beth blames herself and vows never to keep another bird; Amy offers a hopeful, impractical idea; Jo takes charge of the funeral while already overloaded. Some readers find Amy’s suggestion comic, others simply young.
evidence: Put him in the oven, and maybe he will get warm and revive
for I am too bad to own one

days.title: A dinner that became a standing joke — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Follow a long chain of mistakes and decide where the narrator invites laughter and where sympathy.
days.focus: Alcott turns a domestic disaster into comedy without dismissing the loss beneath it.
days.context: Jo has invited Laurie to dinner and must cook it alone. Beth is making a shroud for Pip, whose funeral is planned for the afternoon.
days.contentNote: Pip is buried with tears and a mock-solemn epitaph. The narrator describes the unwelcome guest Miss Crocker with period sharpness as “a thin, yellow spinster.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, Experiments; begins "Leaving the others to console Beth, she departed to the kitchen, which was in a most discouraging st"; ends "afternoon; and a glance at the closet gave her an idea of the success of one part of the experiment.". Complete source paragraphs 1339–1354 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Which choices at the market and in the kitchen set up the dinner’s failure?
facilitatorNotes: She buys a very young lobster, old asparagus and sour strawberries, forgets the bread, boils the asparagus for an hour and refuses further advice. The list shows energy without knowledge.
evidence: after buying a very young lobster, some very old asparagus, and two boxes of acid strawberries
Fearing to ask any more advice, she did her best alone

questions.prompt: How does Laurie behave as a guest, and what does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He talks and laughs to cheer the table, eats the salted berries without complaint, digs Pip’s grave and takes Amy for a drive. His kindness is shown through actions rather than praise.
evidence: he was eating away manfully
Laurie dug a grave under the ferns in the grove

questions.prompt: What turns Jo’s near-tears into laughter at the table?
facilitatorNotes: She meets Laurie’s eyes, which look merry despite his efforts, and suddenly sees the comic side. Shared laughter rescues a moment of embarrassment.
evidence: she met Laurie's eyes, which _would_ look merry in spite of his heroic efforts

questions.prompt: Is Pip’s funeral serious, comic or both? Use the epitaph and the sentence after it.
facilitatorNotes: Tears, moss and violets show real grief, while Beth retiring overcome with emotion and lobster deflates the solemnity. Her grief easing through housework also points toward Mother’s coming lesson.
evidence: Loved and lamented sore,
overcome with emotion and lobster

days.title: Twilight on the porch and a better balance — Little Women excerpt
days.challenge: Evaluate a lesson by connecting its general advice with specific new commitments.
days.focus: A failed experiment leads toward balance rather than abandoning pleasure.
days.context: After the failed dinner, Pip’s funeral and an afternoon of hurried housework, the sisters gather on the porch at twilight. Their mother returns from her own holiday.
days.contentNote: Mrs. March warns the girls not to “delve like slaves” and calls plain cooking an accomplishment “no woman should be without,” expressions of an 1860s household.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, Experiments; begins "Before the housewives could rest, several people called, and there was a scramble to get ready to se"; ends ""We'll remember, mother!" and they did.". Complete source paragraphs 1355–1376 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Beth say the day cannot seem like home? What two absences does she name?
facilitatorNotes: Mother’s withdrawn work and Pip’s death are both results of the experiment, so Beth links comfort with care that someone usually gives.
evidence: It can't seem so without Marmee and little Pip

questions.prompt: What was Mother trying to make visible by taking her own holiday?
facilitatorNotes: She wanted the girls to see that comfort depends on everyone contributing. While she and Hannah covered the missing work, the consequences remained partly hidden.
evidence: the comfort of all depends on each doing her share faithfully

questions.prompt: How do Jo’s and Meg’s new plans respond to what they experienced?
facilitatorNotes: Jo chooses cooking after her failed meal, and Meg takes responsibility for shirts her mother would otherwise sew. Each turns a broad promise into a concrete task.
evidence: I'll learn plain cooking for my holiday task

questions.prompt: Why does Mother warn against the opposite extreme at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The lesson is regular time for useful work and enjoyable play, not endless labor. Her final advice qualifies the girls’ enthusiastic promises to work constantly.
evidence: Have regular hours for work and play

days.title: To the Thawing Wind
days.challenge: Notice where direct requests become physically impossible and interpret the shift.
days.focus: A poet’s invitation to be interrupted by the living world.
days.context: A southwester is wind from the southwest; a hermit lives apart from others. The speaker calls on thawing weather to break through an enclosed room, moving from possible weather effects into fantasy.

questions.prompt: How do the first five commands describe the return of spring?
facilitatorNotes: Rain, nesting birds, dreaming flowers, steaming snow, and exposed brown ground signal renewed activity.
evidence: Find the brown beneath the white

questions.prompt: Where does ordinary thaw become a more startling demand?
facilitatorNotes: Melting window glass exceeds actual weather; it imagines removing the barrier between the speaker and outdoors.
evidence: Melt the glass and leave the sticks

questions.prompt: Why would a poet ask for poems to be scattered?
facilitatorNotes: The disruption can release the speaker from an isolated room into experience. A reader might also hear impatience with work; the ending supports a desire for outward movement.
evidence: Turn the poet out of door.

days.title: A Prayer in Spring
days.challenge: Distinguish attention to the present from certainty about the future.
days.focus: Pleasure, uncertainty, and a compact image of a hovering bird.
days.context: The poem is voiced as a prayer; its religious language frames the speaker’s attention and gratitude.

excerpt.locator:
A Prayer in Spring; source text begins "Oh, give us pleasure in the flowers to-day;
And give us not to think so far away
As the uncerta" and ends "ved for God above
To sanctify to what far ends He will,
But which it only needs that we fulfil.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Boy%27s_Will/A_Prayer_in_Spring

questions.prompt: Why does the prayer ask not to think as far away as harvest?
facilitatorNotes: Harvest is uncertain, while blossoms are present. The speaker asks to enjoy what exists now without claiming the future is unimportant.
evidence: the uncertain harvest

questions.prompt: How does the orchard change between day and night?
facilitatorNotes: Its white blossoms become ghostlike at night. The comparison adds strangeness to beauty rather than merely repeating that the trees are white.
evidence: like ghosts by night

questions.prompt: How can the bird be a meteor and still stand still?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison captures sudden darting followed by hovering near a blossom; the apparently opposing motions make the observation precise.
evidence: in mid air stands still

days.title: I'm nobody! Who are you? (1891 text)
days.challenge: Interpret a speaker’s joke about identity and fame.
days.focus: Privacy, an imagined confidant, and the comic sound of self-advertisement.
days.context: This is the complete poem as printed in the 1891 Second Series edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd. Early editors changed Dickinson’s punctuation and sometimes wording; this reading preserves that historical published version.

excerpt.locator:
I'm nobody! Who are you? (1891 text); source text begins "I'M nobody! Who are you?
Are you nobody, too?
Then there's a pair of us—don't tell!
They'd bani" and ends " to be somebody!
How public, like a frog
To tell your name the livelong day
To an admiring bog!". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems%3A_Second_Series_%28Dickinson%29/I%27m_nobody%21_Who_are_you%3F

questions.prompt: How does the opening question turn nobody into a kind of shared identity?
facilitatorNotes: A second nobody makes a pair and an intimate secret. The paradox gives belonging to people supposedly without public identity.
evidence: Then there's a pair of us

questions.prompt: Why compare a public somebody with a frog?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated announcement of a name resembles repetitive croaking. The bog becomes an audience, making public admiration seem comic.
evidence: To an admiring bog!

questions.prompt: Does the poem prove that all public recognition is dreary?
facilitatorNotes: It offers a playful speaker’s preference, not universal evidence. The reader can enjoy or question the exaggeration while explaining its contrast with private companionship.
evidence: How dreary to be somebody!

days.title: Hope (1891 text)
days.challenge: Trace a metaphor without turning every detail into a literal description.
days.focus: Hope imagined as a persistent gift that asks nothing back.
days.context: Abash means disconcert or make ashamed; extremity means severe difficulty. The 1891 editors gave this poem the title Hope. Read the extended bird comparison across all three stanzas.

excerpt.locator:
Hope (1891 text); source text begins "HOPE is the thing with feathers
That perches in the soul,
And sings the tune without the words," and ends " the chillest land,
And on the strangest sea;
Yet, never, in extremity,
It asked a crumb of me.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems%3A_Second_Series_%28Dickinson%29/Hope

questions.prompt: Why might a tune without words represent hope especially well?
facilitatorNotes: It suggests encouragement that does not depend on a precise explanation or promise. The metaphor places that song within the soul.
evidence: sings the tune without the words

questions.prompt: How does the storm develop the comparison rather than merely change the weather?
facilitatorNotes: The stronger the difficulty, the more valuable the song sounds; a severe storm would be needed to silence it. Weather can stand for hardship.
evidence: sweetest in the gale is heard

questions.prompt: What new quality does the crumb add at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The bird gives warmth and song without demanding payment or nourishment from the speaker. The small concrete word completes the image of an undemanding gift.
evidence: It asked a crumb of me.

days.title: The Railway Train (1891 text)
days.challenge: Maintain an extended comparison while recognizing conflicting traits at its close.
days.focus: Mechanical power, appetite, sound, and obedience.
days.context: A steam train took on water at tanks. Supercilious means looking down on others; Boanerges is a biblical name associated with thunder. The poem imagines machinery as an enormous animal.

excerpt.locator:
The Railway Train (1891 text); source text begins "I LIKE to see it lap the miles,
And lick the valleys up,
And stop to feed itself at tanks;
And " and ends "h like Boanerges;
Then, punctual as a star,
Stop—docile and omnipotent—

questions.prompt: How do lap, lick, and feed change the way the journey appears?
facilitatorNotes: Distance and landscape become things an animal consumes; taking water at tanks fits that appetite.
evidence: lick the valleys up

questions.prompt: What is comic about a train peering into shanties?
facilitatorNotes: A machine becomes a proud, socially judging creature. The elevated railway perspective helps make the personification vivid.
evidence: supercilious, peer

questions.prompt: Why place docile beside omnipotent at the stopping point?
facilitatorNotes: The train seems immensely powerful yet obeys its route and schedule. The stable door returns the final image to a domesticated animal.
evidence: docile and omnipotent

days.title: The Railway Children: waving toward Father
days.challenge: Distinguish a comforting imagined connection from what the children actually know.
days.focus: A repeated gesture turns passing strangers into a possible connection.
days.context: The children avoid the station after the coal incident, but they still watch passing trains and miss their absent father.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, opening through the buns for tea; opens “AFTER the adventure of Peter's Coal-Mine, it seemed well to the children to keep away from the stati”; closes “Whenever an Editor was sensible, there were buns for tea.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the railway matter more here than traffic did at their old home?
facilitatorNotes: The countryside is quiet, and trains seem their remaining link with the lost city life. Naming individual trains makes the unfamiliar setting personal.
evidence: all that was left to link the children to the old life

questions.prompt: What does Phyllis’s “three waves aren’t much” argument reveal about her hope?
facilitatorNotes: She does not insist magic is certain; she thinks the small gesture is worth trying. The returning hand gives real companionship without proving the imagined message reaches Father.
evidence: three waves aren't much

questions.prompt: How does the joke about a “sensible Editor” connect Mother’s work with the children’s daily lives?
facilitatorNotes: An editor becomes sensible when accepting her story; buns mark a paid success. The affectionate family judgment is partial rather than an objective measure of editorial skill.
evidence: Whenever an Editor was sensible, there were buns for tea.

days.title: The Railway Children: two ways to let an offence go
days.challenge: Compare two reconciliations and distinguish apology from avoiding embarrassment.
days.focus: How forgiveness makes a return possible.
days.context: Peter meets the man who caught him taking coal, then brings his sisters back toward the station.
days.contentNote: The quarrel recalls a doll being burned in an earlier game; no human injury is described.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Peter meets the Station Master through the siblings’ reconciliation; opens “One day Peter was going down to the village to get buns to celebrate the sensibleness of the Editor ”; closes ““All right,” said Peter, impatiently, “I'm sorry. There! Now will you come on?””.

questions.prompt: Why does Peter run after someone who has already greeted him politely?
facilitatorNotes: He worries the greeting rests on mistaken identity. Naming the theft and apologising let him accept kindness honestly rather than hiding behind a possible mistake.
evidence: I don't want you to be polite to me if you don't know me

questions.prompt: What mixed feeling about Mother’s cleverness does Peter admit?
facilitatorNotes: He is proud of her stories but misses time playing with her. Her paid work helps the household and costs them some companionship; both feelings can coexist.
evidence: she used to play with us more before she had to be so clever.

questions.prompt: How does Bobbie’s proposed settlement differ from deciding which sibling is completely right?
facilitatorNotes: She admits Phyllis began the teasing yet asks both to withdraw the quarrel. Mutual repair lets them continue together without declaring either wholly innocent.
evidence: both unsay everything since the wave

days.title: The Railway Children: railway lessons and a difficult memory
days.challenge: Follow the change from comic technical talk to feelings partly left unspoken.
days.focus: Different kinds of knowledge: how trains work and what another person feels.
days.context: At the station the children learn machinery terms. At home, their enthusiasm meets Mother’s fear for their safety and memory of her own mother.
days.contentNote: The story lets the children walk on the railway line, and a character makes an inaccurate claim about when emergency equipment may be used. A comic anecdote mentions murder without depicting violence; the family also remembers a deceased grandmother.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, the Porter’s explanations through Mother’s permission; opens “They reached the station and spent a joyous two hours with the Porter. He was a worthy man and seeme”; closes “ctly what it cost her to do it. Only some few of you, like Bobbie, may understand a very little bit.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the Porter a successful teacher for these particular children?
facilitatorNotes: He answers repeated why-questions patiently, gives concrete names and tells memorable stories. The narrator contrasts that patience with some socially higher people.
evidence: never tired of answering the questions that begin with “Why—”

questions.prompt: What does Peter’s response to the other boy’s notebook show about equipment and interest?
facilitatorNotes: He realises he can record numbers without a rich father or identical supplies. Mother’s used black notebook meets the actual need.
evidence: even if he was not the son of a wholesale stationer

questions.prompt: Why does Bobbie understand Mother’s silence differently from Phyllis?
facilitatorNotes: Bobbie senses grief for Granny and imagines grown people still wanting their mothers. Phyllis continues a literal comparison, while Bobbie notices the emotional cost.
evidence: have no mother to run to any more.

days.title: The Railway Children: caring through an anxious night
days.challenge: Infer worry through actions, interrupted sleep and a disagreement about money.
days.focus: Care involves observation and practical limits as well as determination.
days.context: Mother becomes ill. The children want to follow the Doctor’s directions, but the recommended supplies cost more than they have.
days.contentNote: Historical influenza care includes alcohol and special foods. Mother calls for her deceased mother while feverish.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Mother’s influenza through the Doctor sending Bobbie to rest; opens “It was the very next day that Mother had to stay in bed because her head ached so. Her hands were bu”; closes “He was really quite a nice doctor.”.

questions.prompt: How do Mother and the Doctor give Bobbie competing instructions?
facilitatorNotes: The Doctor lists nourishing supplies; Mother rejects their expense and asks for cheaper broth. Bobbie must deal with an affordability problem rather than a simple refusal to care.
evidence: I can't afford all that rubbish

questions.prompt: Why does Phyllis’s comment about dinner money matter to their plan?
facilitatorNotes: Giving up their own food would still not buy everything. Her arithmetic limits a dramatic sacrifice and forces another solution.
evidence: you can't get all those other things with our dinner money.

questions.prompt: What does the Doctor recognise that Bobbie may be overlooking?
facilitatorNotes: She has learned by watching Mother and has worked hard, but exhausted helpers also need food and sleep. His praise is accompanied by instructions that another adult take over.
evidence: We can't afford to have the head-nurse ill.

days.title: The Railway Children: a sign, a letter and a hamper
days.challenge: Follow a message through several people and distinguish payment from freely offered kindness.
days.focus: The limits of judging generosity by money.
days.context: The children have devised a way to ask their regular railway acquaintance for supplies for Mother.
days.contentNote: The hamper includes port wine, reflecting historical ideas about convalescence. Spellings in the children’s letter are part of the source.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, the unusual morning greeting through chapter end; opens “When the 9.15 came out of the tunnel that morning the old gentleman in the first-class carriage put ”; closes “ld me the other day there was a thick hedge of it at her mother's house when she was a little girl.””.

questions.prompt: How do the sign and letter divide the work of getting help?
facilitatorNotes: The large sign catches attention from a moving train; the letter gives the situation, promise of repayment and delivery instructions. The plan uses two different forms for different needs.
evidence: LOOK OUT AT THE STATION

questions.prompt: Why is the Porter hurt by Peter’s mention of twopence?
facilitatorNotes: He has come from concern, bringing sweetbrier as his own gift; Peter assumes a service needing a tip. The polite “No offence” does not erase the narrator’s account of his feeling.
evidence: I wasn't thinking about no tuppences.

questions.prompt: How does the old gentleman anticipate a difficulty that the children only partly acknowledge?
facilitatorNotes: He requires an eventual full explanation to Mother and anticipates her disapproval. His own pleasure in helping does not guarantee her approval of the request.
evidence: When she is well again you must tell her all about it, of course.

days.title: The Railway Children: an apology and two names for a train
days.challenge: Recognise that one person can approve a kindness and disapprove the way it was requested.
days.focus: Different perspectives complicate both a family argument and a familiar train.
days.context: Mother has recovered enough to hear how the children obtained the supplies. Later they visit the Porter, Perks.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, opening through the return home to dinner; opens “WHAT was left of the second sheet and the Brunswick black came in very nicely to make a banner beari”; closes “The children agreed as they went home to dinner that the Porter was most delightful company.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mother apologise for, and what rule does she still defend?
facilitatorNotes: She regrets her anger because the children did not understand, but still insists on privacy and not asking strangers for gifts. An apology need not withdraw every judgment.
evidence: I'm sorry I was so angry

questions.prompt: Why can Mother thank the old gentleman while saying the children acted wrongly?
facilitatorNotes: His generous response and their request are different actions. Students may question Mother’s rule while accurately explaining her distinction.
evidence: not the old gentleman. He was as kind as ever he could be.

questions.prompt: What do “Green Dragon” and “Snail” reveal about the same train?
facilitatorNotes: The children value its appearance and imaginative excitement; railway workers notice lateness. Each nickname selects a different feature rather than changing the actual train.
evidence: We calls her the Snail

days.title: The Railway Children: a special club and a water bridge
days.challenge: Read an adult’s mixed motives alongside a child’s attempt to interpret a family rule.
days.focus: Practical kindness leaves room for another person’s dignity.
days.context: On her birthday Bobbie has sought the Doctor near the canal because she worries about his bill. He offers her a ride. This begins a new excerpt after an intervening scene.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Bobbie climbs into the dog-cart through her happy return; opens “Roberta climbed in and the bony brown horse was made to turn round—which it did not like at all, for”; closes “e she was the one who was right, and she scrambled down the rocky slope with a really happy feeling.”.

questions.prompt: How does Bobbie try to obey Mother’s instruction while still seeking help?
facilitatorNotes: She distinguishes a trusted Doctor from “every one” and asks about joining an existing payment club, rather than simply requesting gifts. Discuss whether that reasoning fits Mother’s intention.
evidence: But you aren't every one, are you?

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator tell us that the Doctor is rather poor too?
facilitatorNotes: It explains his silence and makes his help a real choice with a cost. Readers know more about his feelings than Bobbie does.
evidence: his feelings at that minute were rather mixed.

questions.prompt: How does the aqueduct conversation change the mood and enlarge Bobbie’s understanding?
facilitatorNotes: The Doctor directs attention from worry to a remarkable structure and explains that engineering includes bridges and tunnels. The joke about a bill as long as the aqueduct makes the worry less frightening.
evidence: I thought engineering was making engines.

days.title: The Railway Children: gifts that grow in the giving
days.challenge: Compare spoken thanks with private thoughts and read a celebration alongside its sadness.
days.focus: Generosity can develop during an exchange, rather than arriving fully formed.
days.context: Bobbie returns from her conversation with the Doctor to find the family ready with a birthday surprise.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, the birthday bell through the quiet end of the birthday; opens “Phyllis and Peter met her at the back door. They were unnaturally clean and neat, and Phyllis had a ”; closes “* * * * * * *”.

questions.prompt: Why is the flower map more personal than an ordinary table decoration?

facilitatorNotes: A wink, reassurance, instruction, a safe return arrangement and the repair all show kindness. Students should use behaviour rather than assume accent or manners alone reveal character.

facilitatorNotes: The clear silhouette of a comfortable sleeping bird suggests warmth and enclosure. Wind and sleet then return attention to the travelers’ cold bodies.

facilitatorNotes: Interruptions, repeated phrases, and sobs make the struggle to explain visible. The smallness of his house does not lessen his attachment.

facilitatorNotes: He gives Mole time to recover and pats his shoulder rather than demanding an immediate answer. The quiet support contrasts with his earlier rushing.

facilitatorNotes: The interrupted movement shows testing and correction before confident advance. Finding the way is not a single effortless leap.

evidence: as a swathe of barley is folded

questions.prompt: Why does the conductor first recommend the baggage-master?
facilitatorNotes: He predicts the inventions will attract a crowd and risk damage in the passenger car. His interest includes practical protection.

facilitatorNotes: He walks the length of the train to speak to the engineer after the initial refusal. His willingness to spend effort distinguishes help from a casual promise.

facilitatorNotes: It seems to glory in strength, rush through landscapes and carry him as if flying. Those comparisons convey delight while the mechanism remains a machine.

days.title: Muir’s youth: wooden machines in the Fine Arts Hall

facilitatorNotes: The gatekeeper welcomes him, the hall manager praises their novelty, and he receives a choice of space and carpentry help. Recognition appears in practical arrangements.

questions.prompt: Why does Muir fail to preserve newspaper praise he might otherwise treasure?

facilitatorNotes: The professor remembers the inventions and later connects them with Muir’s writing. What seemed a local display opened relationships and left durable impressions.
