questions.prompt: How does Aietes avoid keeping his promise without openly refusing?
facilitatorNotes: He delays until dark, takes counsel and puts the meeting off until tomorrow, because he fears Jason may kill the serpent too.
evidence: So he delayed, and sat taking counsel with his princes till the sun went down

questions.prompt: Compare the plans of Oileus and Idas with Jason’s choice. Why does Jason hold the crew back?
facilitatorNotes: The crew propose force, and Idas would let the dragon devour one man first. Jason praises their courage but waits, because he hopes for Medeia’s help.
evidence: while the dragon is devouring one, the rest can slay him
for he hoped for Medeia’s help

questions.prompt: What does Medeia give up by agreeing to help, and which words show that she knows it?
facilitatorNotes: Sisters, playfellows and home. Her words accept the choice as fate; students may call it brave, desperate or forced by her father’s threat.
evidence: her heart yearned after her sisters and her playfellows
The lot is cast, and I must endure it.

questions.prompt: Why does Medeia choose Orpheus rather than another warrior to go with Jason?
facilitatorNotes: The serpent cannot be beaten by force, and Orpheus’s music can charm all things. The narrator adds that poets were also bold in those days.
evidence: can charm all things on earth

days.title: Winning the golden fleece — The Heroes excerpt
days.challenge: Notice how sound and silence carry the suspense of a night scene.
days.focus: The fleece is won by guidance, music and nerve together, and the escape releases the tension.
days.context: At midnight Medeia leads Jason and Orpheus to the grove where the fleece hangs, guarded by Brimo, a witch-goddess, and a huge serpent. This is the end of Part IV. The course leaves the Argonauts here; Part V, not included, follows the long voyage home, beginning with Aietes’s pursuit and a crime by Medeia that angers Zeus.
days.contentNote: A lamb is killed as an offering, and Brimo appears with three heads and a pack of hounds. Medeia’s young brother Absyrtus is present but does not act in this passage.

excerpt.locator: The Argonauts, Part IV, How the Argonauts Sailed to Colchis (end); begins "So at midnight they went up the bank, and found Medeia; and beside came Absyrtus her young brother, "; ends "arts rose high again; and they rowed on stoutly and steadfastly, away into the darkness of the West.". Complete source paragraphs 496–509 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why must the lamb be offered before the gates open?
facilitatorNotes: Brimo and her hounds feed at the ditch, then vanish, and the bars and doors give way. The offering works as the price of passage.
evidence: and they ate and drank their fill
and the bars of the gates fell down

questions.prompt: How do sound and silence change as the heroes face the serpent?
facilitatorNotes: His roar shakes the trees and wakes the city; Medeia calls gently, and Orpheus’s song makes the forest still until the serpent breathes like a child.
evidence: roared like the fire among the woodlands
the forest grew calm again

questions.prompt: Who wins the fleece? Use the passage to decide how much belongs to Jason, Medeia and Orpheus.
facilitatorNotes: Medeia guides and calms, Orpheus sings the serpent to sleep, and Jason steps across it and takes the fleece. Defensible answers can stress the shared effort or Jason’s final act.
evidence: Then Jason leapt forward warily, and stept across that mighty snake

questions.prompt: Why might Kingsley repeat the sentence that begins “Into the surge they rushed”?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition imitates the waves and the ship’s leap, like a horse, and marks the moment of escape before the calm sea.
evidence: Into the surge they rushed, and _Argo_ leapt the breakers like a horse

days.title: The stone that would not lift — The Heroes excerpt
days.challenge: Follow time passing through repeated actions and notice a change in their result.
days.focus: A long-awaited achievement raises a new question instead of ending the mystery.
days.context: In a new Greek myth, Theseus grows up with his mother Aithra while his father lives far away. A hidden object will eventually connect them.
days.contentNote: The story includes an absent father, parental sadness and a brief reference to hunting.

excerpt.locator: Theseus, Part I, How Theseus Lifted the Stone; begins "Once upon a time there was a princess in Trœzene, Aithra, the daughter of Pittheus the king. She had"; ends "id, ‘Hide them in your bosom, Theseus my son, and come with me where we can look down upon the sea.’". Complete source paragraphs 650–659 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does repetition make the first failure part of a longer test?
facilitatorNotes: Aithra returns with Theseus each year, and her repeated hopeful response postpones an answer. The time gaps emphasize growth rather than one lucky effort.
evidence: Let it be for another year

questions.prompt: Why does Theseus not simply ask what lies beneath the stone?
facilitatorNotes: He longs to know but sees his mother’s sadness and does not want to distress her. His silence shows concern alongside curiosity.
evidence: her face was so sad that he had not the heart to ask

questions.prompt: Why is his mother’s response surprising when he finally succeeds?
facilitatorNotes: He returns excited with the sword and sandals, but she weeps and asks him to hide them. The objects carry an emotional meaning he does not yet understand.
evidence: Theseus stood by her wondering

days.title: A kingdom seen across the water — The Heroes excerpt
days.challenge: Infer why a parent uses a question about leadership before giving directions.
days.focus: The prospect of power is joined to responsibility and the cost of departure.
days.context: Theseus has found a sword and golden sandals beneath a heavy stone. Aithra takes him to a place overlooking the sea before explaining where he should go.
days.contentNote: Aithra predicts grief, captivity and enslavement in a mythic future, and the passage presents fate as unavoidable.

excerpt.locator: Theseus, Part I, How Theseus Lifted the Stone; begins "Then they went outside the sacred wall, and looked down over the bright blue sea; and Aithra said—"; ends "Then she kissed Theseus, and wept over him; and went into the temple, and Theseus saw her no more.". Complete source paragraphs 660–672 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: How does Aithra’s description make Attica attractive compared with home?
facilitatorNotes: She contrasts a small rocky place with fertile land, silver, marble, flowers and flowing streams. Her detailed praise prepares the question of what he would do as its ruler.
evidence: a land of olive-oil and honey

questions.prompt: What does Theseus’s image of a shepherd suggest about the ruler he hopes to become?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to protect and guide people so they mourn his loss, not merely gain wealth. The image presents leadership as care, though it remains an ambition rather than an achievement.
evidence: the shepherd of his people

questions.prompt: How do the sword and sandals now become more than valuable objects?
facilitatorNotes: Aithra gives a message to accompany them when he meets Ægeus. They are tokens of a prior promise and identity, not simply equipment or treasure.
evidence: The stone is lifted, but whose is the pledge beneath it?

days.title: The longer road and the club-bearer — The Heroes excerpt
days.challenge: Connect a change of route with an unspoken need, then follow how the first adventure tests it.
days.focus: The wish to earn recognition turns a journey into a contest with a man who preys on travellers.
days.context: Aithra has sent Theseus to find Ægeus in Athens. The direct route would be across the bay by ship, but Theseus hesitates before leaving.
days.contentNote: Theseus believes he must earn his absent father’s love through dangerous feats. Periphetes threatens to kill him; in a brief fight Theseus kills Periphetes and leaves the body to the kites and crows.

excerpt.locator: Theseus, Part II, How Theseus Slew the Devourers of Men; begins "So Theseus stood there alone, with his mind full of many hopes. And first he thought of going down t"; ends "er slope, till he came to a broad green valley, and saw flocks and herds sleeping beneath the trees.". Complete source paragraphs 674–694 in the verified transcription index.

questions.prompt: Why does Theseus’s eagerness suddenly give way to doubt?
facilitatorNotes: He wonders whether his father has other sons and whether he will be welcomed after years of absence. Physical distance is no longer his only obstacle.
evidence: What if he will not receive me?

questions.prompt: How does thinking about Heracles give Theseus a plan?
facilitatorNotes: He recalls deeds that relieved people’s suffering and believes comparable achievements will earn his father’s pride. The example connects fame with public benefit, even as his motive remains personal.
evidence: because he rid them of their miseries

questions.prompt: How does the mountain description make the chosen route feel different from the quick sea crossing?
facilitatorNotes: Winding glens, mist, clouds, bogs and a dreary down replace his initial wish for wings. The repeated upward movement makes the cost of his choice concrete.
evidence: there was no road right or left

questions.prompt: Periphetes calls himself a spider and Theseus a fly. How does Theseus answer that comparison in words and in action?
facilitatorNotes: He turns it back by asking where the spider’s fangs are, keeps walking steadily and uses his mantle as a shield. The boast of an inescapable web fails.
evidence: And what is your name among men, bold spider?
But Theseus wrapt his mantle round his left arm quickly

questions.prompt: Why might Kingsley compare Theseus to a sapling during the fight?
facilitatorNotes: A sapling bends under the blows but springs back, suggesting resilience against heavier brute force; the image prepares for his sudden victory.
evidence: like a sapling when the storm is past

days.title: October (A Calendar of Sonnets)
days.challenge: Keep several linked spending and royal images in view.
days.focus: An extravagant seasonal character created by contrast.
days.context: Charily means sparingly; a bier is a stand for a coffin. Jackson imagines seasons as owners of costly colors and frost. October spends their treasures in one great celebration.

excerpt.locator:
October (A Calendar of Sonnets); source text begins "The month of carnival of all the year,
  When Nature lets the wild earth go its way
  And spend" and ends "lue,
  Drinks at a single draught, slow filtered through
  Sunshiny air, as in a tingling wine!".

questions.prompt: How does October differ from spring and summer in its use of color?
facilitatorNotes: Spring holds its colors dear and summer lays out jewels cautiously; October flaunts and burns them. The contrast makes October lavish and brief.
evidence: spend whole seasons on a single day

questions.prompt: Why compare frost to pearls rather than simply calling it white?
facilitatorNotes: Pearls extend the costly treasure imagery and allow a comparison with an empress’s ornaments.
evidence: The winter hoards his pearls of frost

questions.prompt: What does drinking frost as wine add to the carnival image?
facilitatorNotes: It turns a chilly feature into celebration, using sunlit air and a tingling sensation. It is imaginative transformation, not literal drinking.
evidence: as in a tingling wine!

days.title: November (A Calendar of Sonnets)
days.challenge: Separate observed sequence from accusations made through personification.
days.focus: A natural reversal that ends in unanswered ethical questions.
days.context: Sere means dry or withered. A warm return encourages flowers to bloom, followed by frost. The poem gives the month intentions which actual weather does not have.
days.contentNote: The death of flowers is described through burial imagery.

excerpt.locator:
November (A Calendar of Sonnets); source text begins "This is the treacherous month when autumn days
  With summer's voice come bearing summer's gift" and ends "s dwelt.
  What joy sufficient hath November felt?
  What profit from the violet's day of pain?".

questions.prompt: What makes the returning warmth seem trustworthy to the flowers?
facilitatorNotes: It brings summer’s voice and gifts, moistens dusty ground, and encourages renewed blooming. These welcoming details make the reversal sharper.
evidence: With summer's voice come bearing summer's gifts.

questions.prompt: Why is the morning sunshine too late?
facilitatorNotes: It melts the snow but cannot revive the violet. A familiar hopeful image becomes powerless after the freeze.
evidence: Too late to bid the violet live again.

questions.prompt: Does the poem answer its questions about November’s profit?
facilitatorNotes: No. The unanswered questions intensify the speaker’s distress and accusation; readers can discuss the limits of treating weather as a moral agent.
evidence: What profit from the violet's day of pain?

days.title: December (A Calendar of Sonnets)
days.challenge: Explain why a cold season can create both shelter and surprise.
days.focus: Winter as an active maker rather than an empty ending.
days.context: Jackson ends the calendar with ice, hesitant snow, and long nights. Architecture means the structures suggested by frozen water; gird means prepare or strengthen oneself.

excerpt.locator:
December (A Calendar of Sonnets); source text begins "The lakes of ice gleam bluer than the lakes
  Of water 'neath the summer sunshine gleamed:
  Fa" and ends ",
  And every shortening day, as shadows creep
  O'er the brief noontide, fresh surprises find.".

questions.prompt: What makes frozen water more than an absence of movement here?
facilitatorNotes: It constructs arches and bridges while the brook still moves beneath them. Ice becomes an architect.
evidence: its frozen architecture makes

questions.prompt: What two possible explanations does the speaker invent for snow’s coming and going?
facilitatorNotes: The messenger may linger dreamily or reveal a feared message gently. These alternatives make uncertain weather personal and tentative.
evidence: might reveal it by degrees

questions.prompt: How do sleep and surprise fit together at the close?
facilitatorNotes: Long nights offer rest while short days still reveal new things. The year closes with both inward quiet and outward attention.
evidence: fresh surprises find

days.title: Muir’s youth: one flower changes how he sees
days.challenge: Compare surface differences with several structural similarities in a long explanation.
days.focus: Classification becomes a way of seeing relationships.
days.context: A fellow student, Griswold, offers Muir a lesson using a locust-tree flower outside the university dormitory.
days.contentNote: The passage frames nature through Christian belief and describes Muir tasting a locust leaf.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, the first botany lesson through renewed exploration; opens “I received my first lesson in botany from a student by the name of Griswold, who is now County Judge”; closes “t after my regular class tasks were learned; for my eyes never closed on the plant glory I had seen.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Muir initially resist putting locust tree and pea plant in one family?
facilitatorNotes: Their size, hardness and growth habit look profoundly different. His objection lets Griswold distinguish obvious appearance from recurring flower, seed and leaf structures.
evidence: the locust a big, thorny hardwood tree

questions.prompt: How does Griswold build a stronger case than one similar-looking petal would provide?
facilitatorNotes: He compares multiple features: petal arrangement, stamens, pods and leaves. The accumulation supports a pattern of relationship rather than a single coincidence.
evidence: all these similar characters are mere coincidences

questions.prompt: What changes in Muir’s response to flowers after the lesson?
facilitatorNotes: He already loves their beauty, but now actively gathers and studies specimens to understand their relationships. Admiration becomes sustained investigation.
evidence: gathering specimens and keeping them fresh in a bucket in my room

days.title: Muir’s youth: from a scheduled desk to the wilderness
days.challenge: Relate a literal machine and a figurative university without treating either as the whole meaning of education.
days.focus: Learning combines organised study with open-ended exploration.
days.context: Muir recalls his university inventions and the choice to continue learning beyond the university. Illustration captions are excluded as publisher matter.
days.contentNote: The historical devices include automatic flames and a lens that burns thread. The closing account uses religious language about nature.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, the automatic study desk through the final farewell; opens “Nevertheless, I still indulged my love of mechanical inventions. I invented a desk in which the book”; closes “y leaving one University for another, the Wisconsin University for the University of the Wilderness.”.

questions.prompt: How does the desk turn a study plan into a physical sequence?
facilitatorNotes: It presents, opens and removes books according to allotted times. The machinery gives a visible form to his intended routine rather than choosing what matters for him.
evidence: all the day being divided according to the times of recitation

questions.prompt: Why does the janitor’s recognition surprise Muir?
facilitatorNotes: Years have passed and the current janitor did not know him as a student, but Pat’s stories preserved his reputation. An ordinary room carries a remembered history.
evidence: So long had the memory of my little inventions survived.

questions.prompt: What does “the University of the Wilderness” mean in the final sentence?
facilitatorNotes: It treats ongoing observation of nature as another education. His tears and lingering look also show affection for the actual university, so leaving is not a dismissal of it.
evidence: the Wisconsin University for the University of the Wilderness.

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: abundance and exhausting labour
days.challenge: Notice how pleasure and criticism coexist rather than reducing farm life to one judgment.
days.focus: Abundant resources do not automatically create comfortable lives.
days.context: This separate farm-life excerpt places rich harvests beside the labour and discomfort that produced them.
days.contentNote: Describes demanding child labour, painful cold and strict household rules, with Muir’s own criticism of them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, opening through winter hardship and beauty; opens “At first, wheat, corn, and potatoes were the principal crops we raised; wheat especially. But in fou”; closes “ sunsets and white noons, and the cheery, enlivening company of the brave chickadees and nuthatches.”.

questions.prompt: What evidence forces the farmers to change their methods?
facilitatorNotes: Yields fall sharply on exhausted soil; clover ploughed under improves subsequent crops. The account connects an observed problem to a revised practice.
evidence: This caused a complete change in farming methods

questions.prompt: Why does the melon paragraph belong beside accounts of hard work?
facilitatorNotes: Its cold sweetness is intensified by heat and fatigue; the same farm can give both pleasure and strain. The description also returns to soil fertility when a second crop disappoints.
evidence: a glorious luxury that only weary barefooted farm boys can ever know

questions.prompt: What contradiction does Muir expose about the household’s fuel and warmth?
facilitatorNotes: Good wood is abundant yet treated as an obstacle to farming, while the family huddles round an inadequate stove. He criticises a failure to turn available resources into humane comfort.
evidence: The very best oak and hickory fuel was embarrassingly abundant

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: winter’s changing theatre
days.challenge: Connect visual and sound imagery while separating an event from its interpretation.
days.focus: Beauty and alarm can arise from the same cold landscape.
days.context: After describing farm hardship, Muir recalls sights and sounds that made winter memorable.
days.contentNote: Father interprets the aurora through Christian belief. The boys walk on frozen lakes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, the stars and aurora through the sounds of lake ice; opens “The winter stars far surpassed those of our stormy Scotland in brightness, and we gazed and gazed as”; closes “n ahead of us, creaking and whooping as if all the ice eighteen or twenty inches thick was breaking.”.

questions.prompt: How do the robe and folds make the aurora imaginable?
facilitatorNotes: They give shifting coloured light a familiar shape. Father extends the image into religious interpretation, which is distinct from the visible light itself.
evidence: All the sky is clad in a robe of red light.

questions.prompt: Why can the ice storm be both destructive and beautiful in this account?
facilitatorNotes: Its weight breaks branches, yet the remaining wood shines as if made of crystal. The writer preserves both effects rather than making beauty mean harmlessness.
evidence: many of them lost a third or more of their branches

questions.prompt: How does the last paragraph change the reader’s experience from the earlier distant sky?
facilitatorNotes: Sound seems to move immediately beneath the boys’ feet, making them afraid. The narrator gives expansion and contraction as a cause while recalling their first impression of breaking ice.
evidence: the sudden rumbling roar beneath our feet

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: what lies beneath an open field
days.challenge: Follow the shift from a practical tool problem to an explanation across many years.
days.focus: Careful observation reveals a landscape’s hidden history.
days.context: Muir describes preparing new farmland and the roots that resisted the plough, then explains how fire shaped the landscape.
days.contentNote: The passage describes settlers transforming land and does not discuss Indigenous land management. Scottish speech and a mild dialect exclamation are retained.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, the breaking plough through the vanished oak openings; opens “By this time I had learned to run the breaking plough. Most of these ploughs were very large, turnin”; closes “o dense that it was difficult to walk through them and every trace of the sunny “openings” vanished.”.

questions.prompt: Why does strength alone fail to keep the neighbour’s plough in the ground?
facilitatorNotes: The tool is poorly adjusted. Sharp, correctly set parts cut the roots, while brute force cannot compensate for that fault.
evidence: who did not know how to trim it

questions.prompt: How can a root be over a century old while its visible shoots are very young?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated fires kill the shoots but leave the root alive to sprout again. The passage separates the age of the organism’s surviving parts from the age of what is above ground.
evidence: the root continued to hold on to life

questions.prompt: What later change supports Muir’s explanation of the open woodland?
facilitatorNotes: When running grass fires are prevented, persistent roots grow into dense thickets and the openings disappear. The observation supports a role for fire, while this historical account is not a complete modern ecological study.
evidence: every trace of the sunny “openings” vanished.

days.title: Muir’s boyhood: ninety feet of sandstone
days.challenge: Separate the facts of an accident from the judgment the writer quietly makes about it.
days.focus: Muir’s plain account lets details, not complaint, carry his view of his father’s demands.
days.context: Continuing directly from the account of the oak openings, Muir turns to the family’s second farm, which had no spring or stream, so a well had to be dug through rock. An illustration caption between the two passages is omitted.
days.contentNote: Muir nearly dies from carbon dioxide gas (“choke-damp”) at the bottom of the well his father set him to dig; a neighbor calls his survival God’s mercy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, the Hickory Hill well; opens “We called our second farm Hickory Hill, from its many fine hickory trees and the long gentle slope l”; closes “ covered top over it, and swung two iron-bound buckets in it from which we all drank for many a day.”.

questions.prompt: Why was the well dug by hand with chisels, and what were Muir’s working conditions?
facilitatorNotes: Blasting by inexperienced men went too slowly, so his father gave him the work: cramped, alone and below ground from morning to dark for months.
evidence: from lack of skill the blasting went on very slowly
I had to sit cramped in a space about three feet in diameter

questions.prompt: What does Muir say saved him at the bottom of the shaft?
facilitatorNotes: A glimpse of a bur-oak branch over the opening wakes him enough to answer and climb into the bucket. Some readers note that a tree, not a person, rouses him.
evidence: I happened to catch a glimpse of a branch of a bur-oak tree

questions.prompt: What did William Duncan know that Muir’s father did not, and what changed afterward?
facilitatorNotes: As a miner he knew the danger of choke-damp and how to clear it, with water, a moving bundle and a candle test. The work resumes with those precautions.
evidence: Mr. Duncan taught father to throw water down the shaft
test the air with a candle

questions.prompt: What does the short sentence “Father never spent an hour in that well” add after the proverb about chipping?
facilitatorNotes: Muir twists the proverb to say the work wore him down, then states a plain fact about his father. Readers may hear criticism, pride in his own skill, or both.
evidence: wearing away the chipper
Father never spent an hour in that well.

days.title: Mowing
days.challenge: Keep the speaker’s uncertainty separate from the poem’s stronger concluding claim.
days.focus: Labor, imagined voices, and the satisfaction of making something real.
days.context: A scythe is a long curved blade for cutting grass; a swale is a low stretch of land; a fay is a fairy. The speaker listens to work and considers what its sound might mean.

excerpt.locator:
Mowing; source text begins "There was never a sound beside the wood but one,
And that was my long scythe whispering to the " and ends "fact is the sweetest dream that labor knows.
My long scythe whispered and left the hay to make.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Boy%27s_Will/Mowing

questions.prompt: Why does the poem ask what the scythe whispered and then say the speaker does not know?
facilitatorNotes: The opening invites interpretation but qualifies it. Perhaps repeats that uncertainty rather than reporting an actual spoken message.
evidence: I knew not well myself

questions.prompt: What sort of dream does the speaker reject?
facilitatorNotes: A reward arriving through idle time or magical gold. The contrast prepares a different dream grounded in earnest work.
evidence: easy gold at the hand of fay or elf

questions.prompt: How does the final action help explain the claim about fact and dream?
facilitatorNotes: The cut grass is left to become hay: real work produces a material result. Readers can debate whether the pleasure is achievement, attention, or both.
evidence: left the hay to make

days.title: The Wind's Visit (1891 text)
days.challenge: Notice where a sustained human comparison breaks down and becomes more inventive.
days.focus: An invisible presence made vivid through gestures and sound.
days.context: Countenance means face; a billow is a swelling wave. The speaker welcomes wind as a visitor, then finds that ordinary rules of hospitality cannot fully apply to it.

excerpt.locator:
The Wind's Visit (1891 text); source text begins "THE wind tapped like a tired man,
And like a host, "Come in,"
I boldly answered; entered then
M" and ends " still flitting;
Then, like a timid man,
Again he tapped—’t was flurriedly—
And I became alone.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems%3A_Second_Series_%28Dickinson%29/The_Wind%27s_Visit

questions.prompt: Why does the offer of a chair expose a problem with treating wind as a person?
facilitatorNotes: A footless, boneless guest cannot sit as a person does. The impossible sofa makes the comparison playful instead of mechanically exact.
evidence: A sofa to the air

questions.prompt: Which two sound comparisons give the guest a voice?
facilitatorNotes: Hummingbirds suggest a rapid humming rush, while trembling glass suggests a more delicate musical tone. Both make movement audible.
evidence: Blown tremulous in glass

questions.prompt: What changes between the first and last descriptions of a man?
facilitatorNotes: The visitor first seems tired and later timid or hurried. The speaker is left alone, giving this brief natural event the shape of a social encounter.
evidence: And I became alone.

days.title: Lamb’s Midsummer Night’s Dream: two disputes enter one wood
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Keep two groups of characters distinct while recognising a shared conflict about control.
days.focus: The wood brings human and fairy disagreements together.
days.context: Mary Lamb retells Shakespeare’s comedy in prose. This opening introduces four young Athenians and the fairy rulers of the wood.
days.contentNote: Includes a threatened execution for refusing an arranged marriage, a quarrel over a stolen child and controlling behaviour.

excerpt.locator: “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” opening through Oberon’s threat; opens “There was a law in the city of Athens which gave to its citizens the power of compelling their daugh”; closes “er. "Well, go your way," said Oberon: "before the morning dawns I will torment you for this injury."”.

questions.prompt: What practical feature of the proposed journey gives Hermia and Lysander hope?
facilitatorNotes: The cruel law applies only within Athens, so the aunt’s home offers a place beyond its reach. Their plan responds to a boundary of authority, not simply a desire for scenery.
evidence: this law not extending beyond the boundaries of the city

questions.prompt: Why does Helena tell Demetrius a secret entrusted to her?
facilitatorNotes: She hopes to follow him when he pursues Hermia, though she gains no promise of affection. The narrator criticises a choice that places her longing above friendship.
evidence: the poor pleasure of following her faithless lover to the wood

questions.prompt: What do the elves hiding in acorn-cups reveal about Oberon and Titania’s quarrel?
facilitatorNotes: The dispute affects their attendants, who fear the rulers despite the tiny, charming setting. Fairy life is not presented as free from power or conflict.
evidence: hide themselves for fear

days.title: Lamb’s Midsummer Night’s Dream: a charm and a lullaby
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Compare a character’s helpful intention in one situation with manipulation in another.
days.focus: A protective song gains irony from what the reader knows.
days.context: Oberon plans to use a flower’s magic on Titania. While waiting for Puck, he overhears Helena and Demetrius.
days.contentNote: Puck’s pranks include making an old woman fall, and Oberon’s charm controls Titania’s affection without her knowledge; the narrator calls such acts merry.

excerpt.locator:
“A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” Puck’s introduction through Oberon’s spell; opens “Oberon then sent for Puck, his chief favourite and privy counsellor.”; closes “"What thou seest when thou dost wake,
Do it for thy true-love take."”.

questions.prompt: How do Puck’s village pranks prepare us to judge his suitability for a delicate task?
facilitatorNotes: They show cleverness and speed but also delight in other people’s discomfort. A reader can anticipate trouble without assuming he will deliberately disobey.
evidence: a shrewd and knavish sprite

questions.prompt: What weakness in Oberon’s directions might allow Puck to choose the wrong person?
facilitatorNotes: Athenian clothing is a broad clue, not a unique identity. Oberon also assumes the beloved woman will be the first person seen on waking.
evidence: You will know the man by the Athenian garments

questions.prompt: Why is the lullaby’s wish about spells especially ironic?
facilitatorNotes: The fairies ask that no charm approach their queen just before Oberon secretly applies one. Readers know the danger comes from someone outside the animals named in the song.
evidence: Never harm, nor spell, nor charm,

days.title: Lamb’s Midsummer Night’s Dream: praise heard as mockery
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Explain one event differently from the perspectives of a reader and an uninformed character.
days.focus: False explanations can injure a real friendship.
days.context: Puck has been told to charm an Athenian man so that he will return Helena’s love. Hermia and Lysander are also resting in the same wood.
days.contentNote: The retelling repeats the threat against Hermia and makes a dated generalisation about men being better runners.

excerpt.locator: “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” the sleeping lovers through the friends’ quarrel; opens “But to return to Hermia, who made her escape out of her father's house that night, to avoid the deat”; closes “her, and hold the sweet jest up. If you had any pity, grace, or manners, you would not use me thus."”.

questions.prompt: Which clues lead Puck to his mistaken identification?
facilitatorNotes: He sees Athenian clothes and a young woman nearby, matching the broad instructions. The clues fit the wrong couple, showing why a plausible inference can still fail.
evidence: concluded that this must be the Athenian maid and her disdainful lover

questions.prompt: Why does Helena hear admiration as cruelty rather than welcome affection?
facilitatorNotes: She knows Lysander is promised to Hermia and knows Demetrius has rejected her. Without knowledge of magic, mockery seems more likely than two sudden changes of heart.
evidence: were all in a plot together to make a jest of her

questions.prompt: What does the “double cherry” memory add to Helena’s accusation?
facilitatorNotes: It pictures long intimacy and shared work, making the supposed betrayal hurt more. The image also contrasts their former closeness with the present divided understanding.
evidence: growing up together in fashion of a double cherry

days.title: Lamb’s Midsummer Night’s Dream: putting the mischief right
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Track two separate uses of magic and weigh the narrator’s comic framing against their effects.
days.focus: Repairing a mistake does not erase questions about how power was used.
days.context: The mistaken enchantments have made the lovers quarrel. Oberon orders Puck to prevent a fight, then turns back to Titania.
days.contentNote: Includes a prevented duel and an enchantment used to pressure Titania. “Ass” means donkey here.

excerpt.locator: “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” the men depart to fight through the fairy reconciliation; opens “While Helena and Hermia were speaking these angry words to each other, Demetrius and Lysander left t”; closes “ers, and their midnight quarrels; and she agreed to go with him and see the end of their adventures.”.

questions.prompt: How will Puck’s imitated voices prevent the duel rather than cause it?
facilitatorNotes: Each man follows a false rival through fog until exhausted; keeping them apart removes the opportunity to fight. The same talent for deception serves a different immediate purpose.
evidence: they shall not be able to find each other

questions.prompt: What does the transformed clown want most from his extraordinary attendants?
facilitatorNotes: He asks for scratching, simple food and sleep rather than royal splendour. His ordinary bodily wishes contrast with Titania’s extravagant praise and offers.
evidence: I had rather have a handful of dried pease

questions.prompt: Does Oberon remove Titania’s enchantment simply because he regrets it?
facilitatorNotes: He first gains the boy he wanted, then releases her. Students can recognise the reconciled ending while questioning the pressure used to produce it.
evidence: having thus obtained the little boy he had so long wished for

days.title: Lamb’s Midsummer Night’s Dream: waking to a changed world
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Distinguish a resolved plot from complete knowledge of how its resolution happened.
days.focus: The dream frame invites readers to reconsider the comedy’s disturbances.
days.context: Puck has removed Lysander’s mistaken enchantment. The four Athenians wake together, while Oberon and Titania watch unseen.
days.contentNote: The ending recalls the threatened execution, which does not take place; the narrator calls the dream “harmless.”

excerpt.locator: “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” the sleepers are found through the tale’s ending; opens “The fairy king and queen found the lovers and their fair ladies, at no great distance from each othe”; closes “my readers will be so unreasonable as to be offended with a pretty harmless Midsummer Night's Dream.”.

questions.prompt: Why do Hermia and Lysander wonder whether the night was a shared dream?
facilitatorNotes: They remember strange changes but cannot see the fairy causes. Their uncertainty differs from the reader’s fuller explanation.
evidence: dreaming the same bewildering dream

questions.prompt: What changes Egeus’s decision about Hermia’s marriage?
facilitatorNotes: Demetrius no longer wishes to marry her, so the father ceases opposing Lysander. The immediate demand changes; the passage does not say the cruel law itself has been abolished.
evidence: Demetrius would not now marry his daughter

questions.prompt: What does the final invitation to think of a dream ask the reader to do?
facilitatorNotes: It asks readers to accept impossible events and forgive the entertainment. They may enjoy that invitation while debating whether every prank was as harmless as the narrator claims.
evidence: a pretty harmless Midsummer Night's Dream

days.title: Going for Water
days.challenge: Track changes in pace and sense perception across six short stanzas.
days.focus: An ordinary need becomes a shared discovery.
days.context: Two people leave a dry well to seek a brook on an autumn evening. Loth means reluctant; ere means before. The poem turns a necessary errand into play and then concentrated listening.

excerpt.locator:
Going for Water; source text begins "The well was dry beside the door,
    And so we went with pail and can
Across the fields behind" and ends "ling fall that made
Now drops that floated on the pool
    Like pearls, and now a silver blade.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Boy%27s_Will/Going_for_Water

questions.prompt: Are the walkers disappointed to have to seek water elsewhere?
facilitatorNotes: Not entirely: they welcome an excuse to go out on a fair evening. Necessity and pleasure coexist.
evidence: Not loth to have excuse to go

questions.prompt: How does the moon change roles as the walkers enter the woods?
facilitatorNotes: First they seem to run to meet it; then they play at hiding from it. Personification turns the walk into a game.
evidence: Like gnomes that hid us from the moon

questions.prompt: Why do they stop one another before looking at the brook?
facilitatorNotes: Their joined hush lets them hear it first. The final pearls and silver blade then translate its changing movement into visual forms.
evidence: To listen ere we dared to look

days.title: Lamb’s As You Like It: friendship in exile and at court
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Compare a figurative response to hardship with practical acts of loyalty.
days.focus: People can choose relationships differently from their rulers.
days.context: Mary Lamb’s retelling begins with two brothers divided by power and two cousins whose friendship survives that division.
days.contentNote: Mentions killing deer for food and an old belief about a medicinal jewel in a toad’s head. The latter is a historical literary image, not a natural-history fact.

excerpt.locator: “As You Like It,” opening through the invitation to the wrestling match; opens “During the time that France was divided into provinces (or dukedoms as they were called) there reign”; closes “o the court before the palace; and Celia, thinking it would amuse Rosalind, agreed to go and see it.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the duke’s forest companions different from people merely driven from court?
facilitatorNotes: They choose exile for his sake, losing land and income. The voluntary cost makes their presence evidence of loyalty.
evidence: put themselves into a voluntary exile for his sake

questions.prompt: Why does the duke call cold winds “true counsellors”?
facilitatorNotes: They plainly reveal his condition, unlike flattering people at court. The comparison helps him find something useful in discomfort without claiming the cold is pleasant.
evidence: they do not flatter

questions.prompt: How does Celia respond to the wrong her father has done?
facilitatorNotes: She comforts Rosalind and tries to make amends through kindness rather than copying her father’s hostility. Their closeness crosses the division between the adults.
evidence: the disagreement between their fathers did not in the least interrupt

days.title: Lamb’s As You Like It: the wrestling match
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Track how a public contest becomes a private turning point for two characters.
days.focus: Mary Lamb compresses Shakespeare’s scene so that sympathy, courage and love grow in a few paragraphs.
days.context: Celia and Rosalind have agreed to watch a wrestling match at the court of Frederick, the duke who banished Rosalind’s father.
days.contentNote: The court wrestler is said to have killed many men in earlier contests and is badly hurt in this one. The narrator remarks that wrestling is now practised only “by country clowns,” a period class judgment.

excerpt.locator: “As You Like It,” the wrestling match through Celia’s question to Rosalind; opens “In those times wrestling, which is only practised now by country clowns”; closes “for my father hated his father; yet I do not hate Orlando.””.

questions.prompt: Why does the duke ask the ladies to speak to the young stranger, and what happens instead?
facilitatorNotes: He expects the young man to be killed and hopes they can dissuade him. Their kindness makes Orlando more determined to show courage.
evidence: I would wish to persuade him from wrestling
all his thoughts were bent to distinguish himself by his courage

questions.prompt: What in Orlando’s speech makes Rosalind think he is “like herself”?
facilitatorNotes: He says he has no friends to lament him and is willing to die. Rosalind, whose father is banished, recognises misfortune like her own, and sympathy turns into love.
evidence: for I have none to lament me
made Rosalind think that he was like herself, unfortunate

questions.prompt: How does one fact about Orlando’s father produce opposite reactions in Frederick and Rosalind?
facilitatorNotes: Sir Rowland was a friend of the banished duke. Frederick’s liking turns to displeasure, while Rosalind is delighted. The same fact tests loyalty in two directions.
evidence: all his liking for this brave young man was changed into displeasure
My father loved Sir Rowland de Boys

questions.prompt: What do Rosalind’s gift of the chain and her words with it tell Orlando and the reader?
facilitatorNotes: She has lost fortune and position but gives what she can; the gift says more than her polite words. Celia then names what the reader suspects.
evidence: I am out of suits with fortune
Is it possible you should fall in love so suddenly?

days.title: Lamb’s As You Like It: choosing to leave together
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Track the cousins’ real identities, chosen names and changing practical needs.
days.focus: Loyalty becomes action when comfort and rank must be left behind.
days.context: After Orlando wins the wrestling match, Frederick’s resentment of his banished brother’s friends grows, and he turns against Rosalind.
days.contentNote: The narrator presents courage as masculine and calls a woman “the weaker vessel,” a common phrase of the period.

excerpt.locator: “As You Like It,” Frederick’s banishment of Rosalind through the shepherd cottage; opens “Frederick being enraged at the sight of Sir Rowland de Boys' son, which reminded him of the many fri”; closes “ed that Orlando was also in the forest of Arden: and in this manner this strange event came to pass.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Frederick think Celia should welcome Rosalind’s removal?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines public admiration as a competition: Celia will seem better without her cousin. Celia instead values companionship, refusing that rivalry.
evidence: you will seem more bright and virtuous when she is gone

questions.prompt: What do the disguises solve, and what do they fail to solve?
facilitatorNotes: They hide rank and are intended to make travel safer, but do not supply food, directions or endurance. The collapse of forced courage shows their practical limits.
evidence: feigned manliness and forced courage would no longer support them

questions.prompt: Why does buying the cottage change their situation more securely than a brave speech?
facilitatorNotes: It provides shelter, food and a local helper while they search for the duke. Their recovery depends on resources and assistance as well as determination.
evidence: well supplied with provisions

days.title: Lamb’s As You Like It: asking instead of taking
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Follow a change from threat to trust and compare two people’s sacrifices.
days.focus: Care reverses the expected direction of service.
days.context: Orlando also reaches the forest, fleeing his brother with the elderly servant Adam. This excerpt explains their danger and their need for help.
days.contentNote: Includes a brother’s threat to burn Orlando’s room, extreme hunger and a drawn sword; no attack is carried out in this excerpt.

excerpt.locator: “As You Like It,” Orlando’s family history through the duke’s welcome; opens “Orlando was the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys, who, when he died, left him (Orlando being then”; closes “he took him under his protection, and Orlando and his old servant lived with the duke in the forest.”.

questions.prompt: What makes Adam’s offer of money a substantial sacrifice?
facilitatorNotes: It is the savings intended to support his own old age. He gives up security to protect Orlando, not spare change with no other purpose.
evidence: laid by to be provision for me when my old limbs should become unfit for service

questions.prompt: What assumption leads Orlando to draw his sword, and what overturns it?
facilitatorNotes: He expects savagery in the forest and tries force; the duke’s gentle welcome proves he can ask for human courtesy. His shame marks recognition of the mistaken assumption.
evidence: I thought that all things had been savage here

questions.prompt: Why does Orlando refuse to eat immediately when food is offered?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers exhausted Adam and will not satisfy himself first. Carrying the servant back reverses their usual roles and shows reciprocal loyalty.
evidence: till he be satisfied, I must not touch a bit.

days.title: Lamb’s As You Like It: a disguise tested by feeling
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Distinguish what a disguised character means from what other people hear.
days.focus: Pretending offers freedom until real danger breaks through the performance.
days.context: Rosalind is disguised as Ganymede, while Celia uses Aliena. Orlando does not know that the shepherd he meets is Rosalind herself.
days.contentNote: Includes a lioness killed as she attacks and a bleeding arm, briefly described.

excerpt.locator: “As You Like It,” the lovers meet in the forest through Ganymede’s faint; opens “Orlando arrived in the forest not many days after Ganymede and Aliena came there, and (as has been b”; closes “terfeit to be a man." "So I do," replied Ganymede, truly," but I should have been a woman by right."”.

questions.prompt: Why is the proposed cure for love a secret joke for Rosalind?
facilitatorNotes: Orlando practises courting Rosalind while speaking to Rosalind herself. The stated aim of curing love hides her pleasure in hearing it expressed.
evidence: these fine love-speeches were all addressed to the right person

questions.prompt: What makes Orlando’s rescue of Oliver more than an ordinary act of courage?
facilitatorNotes: He recognises a brother who planned to harm him and briefly feels tempted to leave, then chooses rescue. The hesitation makes forgiveness a choice rather than automatic affection.
evidence: brotherly affection and the gentleness of his nature soon overcame his first anger

questions.prompt: Why does Oliver doubt that Ganymede’s faint was merely acting?
facilitatorNotes: Physical paleness suggests a real response, while the reader knows Rosalind’s fear for Orlando. Her answer about being a woman is true in a way Oliver cannot understand.
evidence: Oliver saw by the paleness of his complexion that he did really faint

days.title: Lamb’s As You Like It: a promise that needs no magic
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Notice how a promise can sound impossible to one listener and straightforward to another.
days.focus: Recognition, restitution and friendship complete different parts of the ending.
days.context: Oliver and Celia wish to marry. Still disguised as Ganymede, Rosalind promises that Orlando may marry Rosalind on the same day.
days.contentNote: The ending reports an abandoned plan to kill the exiled duke and interprets repentance through religious belief. No such attack occurs.

excerpt.locator: “As You Like It,” Oliver’s return through the tale’s ending; opens “Oliver made this visit a very long one, and when at last he returned back to his brother, he had muc”; closes “ortune, were very well pleased to return in peace and prosperity to the palace of their lawful duke.”.

questions.prompt: Why can Ganymede promise Rosalind’s arrival with complete confidence?
facilitatorNotes: The supposed magic is a change of clothes and disclosure of identity. The audience’s knowledge turns the promise into dramatic irony.
evidence: quickly became Rosalind without the power of magic

questions.prompt: What action makes Frederick’s reported repentance more than an expression of regret?
facilitatorNotes: He offers to restore the dukedom and the followers’ land and revenue. The tale presents restitution as a visible consequence of his changed intention.
evidence: offer to restore to him his dukedom

questions.prompt: How does Celia’s response to the restored dukedom echo her earlier choice to leave court?
facilitatorNotes: She sincerely celebrates Rosalind’s gain even though she herself loses the expected inheritance. Friendship again outweighs the competition her father assumed.
evidence: though she herself was no longer heir to the dukedom

days.title: The Tuft of Flowers
days.challenge: Distinguish observed evidence from an inference about an absent person’s motive.
days.focus: How a small spared patch revises a conviction about solitude.
days.context: One worker comes to turn grass after another has mowed it. A whetstone sharpens a blade. The worker does not meet the mower; the poem follows an interpretation of the trace he has left.

excerpt.locator:
The Tuft of Flowers; source text begins "I went to turn the grass once after one
Who mowed it in the dew before the sun." and ends "'Men work together,' I told him from the heart,
'Whether they work together or apart.'". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Boy%27s_Will/The_Tuft_of_Flowers

questions.prompt: What belief about work does the speaker hold before following the butterfly?
facilitatorNotes: Even people working together are ultimately alone. The absent mower and quiet scene support that initial feeling without proving it universally.
evidence: Whether they work together or apart.

questions.prompt: Which part of the mower’s motive is observed, and which part is inferred?
facilitatorNotes: The uncut flowers are observable. Loving them from sheer gladness rather than to impress others is the speaker’s interpretation; it is plausible but not confirmed by conversation.
evidence: By leaving them to flourish, not for us

questions.prompt: What changes between the first and final statements about working together or apart?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated phrase now supports fellowship instead of isolation. The speaker feels a kindred mind through the work, though the mower remains physically absent.
evidence: Men work together

days.title: The Snake (1891 text)
days.challenge: Separate familiar observation from an involuntary feeling that the observer cannot explain away.
days.focus: A hidden creature, mistaken recognition, and bodily fear.
days.context: This is the early published version, whose wording differs from some modern editions. A whip-lash is a flexible strip attached to a whip; cordiality means warm friendliness. Read how the speaker identifies an animal through its movement.
days.contentNote: The poem recalls fear of a snake without injury or graphic description.

excerpt.locator:
The Snake (1891 text); source text begins "A NARROW fellow in the grass
Occasionally rides;
You may have met him,—did you not,
His notice " and ends "ut never met this fellow,
Attended or alone,
Without a tighter breathing,
And zero at the bone.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems%3A_Second_Series_%28Dickinson%29/The_Snake

questions.prompt: Why is a comb a useful image for the animal’s passage?
facilitatorNotes: The grass divides and closes in a narrow moving line, as teeth separate strands. The animal is revealed indirectly through its surroundings.
evidence: The grass divides as with a comb

questions.prompt: How does the childhood mistake make the sudden movement startling?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker first sees an object to pick up, then discovers living motion as it wrinkles away. The shift overturns an apparently safe interpretation.
evidence: It wrinkled, and was gone.

questions.prompt: Why mention friendliness toward other creatures before the final coldness?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes that this fear is a particular exception. Tighter breathing and zero at the bone describe a bodily reaction, not evidence that every snake is dangerous.
evidence: zero at the bone

days.title: Lamb’s Comedy of Errors: a family divided by the sea
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Keep two pairs of twins and their separations clear within a story told inside another story.
days.focus: A search for family brings both hope and danger.
days.context: Mary Lamb retells a comedy whose opening is grave: an old traveller faces a cruel law and explains why he has risked entering Ephesus.
days.contentNote: Includes a threatened execution, a shipwreck and a grieving man saying he does not fear death. Children are bought as enslaved attendants in the story.

excerpt.locator: “The Comedy of Errors,” opening through Ægeon’s day of grace; opens “The states of Syracuse and Ephesus being at variance, there was a cruel law made at Ephesus, ordaini”; closes “ess and hopeless of any relief, he retired from the presence of the duke in the custody of a jailor.”.

questions.prompt: How does the storm divide the six family members and attendants into two groups?
facilitatorNotes: One parent is tied near each son and one attendant; the broken ship separates the two supported groups. Drawing the arrangement can clarify why each survivor knows only part of what happened.
evidence: we bound ourselves separately to these masts with the children

questions.prompt: Why does Ægeon reluctantly permit the younger son’s search?
facilitatorNotes: He longs for news of those already lost but fears losing those still with him. The decision holds two competing forms of care, not a lack of affection.
evidence: in sending my younger one to find them, I hazarded the loss of him also

questions.prompt: Why does the duke’s extra day seem almost useless to Ægeon?
facilitatorNotes: He needs a large sum but knows no one he can ask in the city. Sympathy changes the deadline while leaving the practical obstacle in place.
evidence: not knowing any man in Ephesus

days.title: Lamb’s Comedy of Errors: the wrong man called to dinner
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Use the city labels to track identity while characters rely on familiar faces.
days.focus: The reader’s extra knowledge turns confusion into dramatic irony.
days.context: Both brothers are named Antipholus and both attendants Dromio. One pair lives in Ephesus; the other has just arrived from Syracuse.
days.contentNote: The passage describes enslavement, and Antipholus beats the blameless Dromio, the kind of slapstick violence common in Elizabethan comedy.

excerpt.locator: “The Comedy of Errors,” both sons in Ephesus through the mistaken dinner; opens “Ægeon supposed he knew no person in Ephesus; but at the very time he was in danger of losing his lif”; closes “ no less surprised, for the cook-maid, who was his brother's wife, also claimed him for her husband.”.

questions.prompt: What does the reader know that makes Ægeon’s hopelessness especially ironic?
facilitatorNotes: Both sons are nearby, and the established son could afford the ransom. Separation now depends on missing knowledge rather than physical distance.
evidence: both in the city of Ephesus

questions.prompt: Why do Antipholus and the first Dromio each think the other is joking?
facilitatorNotes: Each sees the likeness of his familiar companion, but they refer to different facts: money sent to an inn versus a wife’s dinner summons. Neither yet considers a twin.
evidence: Now it was not his own Dromio

questions.prompt: How does the final dinner deepen the mistake instead of settling it?
facilitatorNotes: Two women confidently identify the visitor as family, and even Dromio is claimed as a husband. Repeated agreement seems persuasive while all the identifications share the same false basis.
evidence: the cook-maid, who was his brother's wife, also claimed him for her husband.

days.title: Lamb’s Comedy of Errors: a chain follows the wrong brother
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Track an object and a payment across several mistaken identifications.
days.focus: Sincere testimony can conflict when people lack one crucial fact.
days.context: The visiting Antipholus has dined in his brother’s house. The real resident returns and finds himself locked out.
days.contentNote: Includes imprisonment for debt, accusations of witchcraft and the coercive master–servant relationship of the historical story.

excerpt.locator: “The Comedy of Errors,” the locked door through the second lady’s demand; opens “While Antipholus of Syracuse was dining with his brother's wife, his brother, the real husband, retu”; closes “ him for his brother: the married Antipholus had done all the things she taxed this Antipholus with.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the servants feel certain they should not admit the men at the door?
facilitatorNotes: They believe those very people are already inside and are obeying the mistress’s order. Their confidence depends on confusing identity with appearance.
evidence: Antipholus was at dinner with their mistress

questions.prompt: How can the goldsmith and the arrested Antipholus both believe they are telling the truth?
facilitatorNotes: The goldsmith really handed over the chain, but to the twin; the resident really never received it. The missing distinction makes honest recollections appear incompatible.
evidence: they disputed this matter a long time, both thinking they were right

questions.prompt: Why does the visiting Antipholus begin to believe in sorcery?
facilitatorNotes: Strangers know his name and claim shared events he does not remember. It is an understandable explanation from limited evidence, while the reader can explain it without magic.
evidence: we wander here in illusions

days.title: Lamb’s Comedy of Errors: certainty becomes confinement
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Test a confident explanation against evidence available to the reader.
days.focus: Protective intentions and confident judgments can both go wrong.
days.context: A second lady reports that Antipholus has behaved strangely. Adriana combines this with the puzzling events she has witnessed.
days.contentNote: Contains period terms such as “lunatic”: Antipholus is wrongly bound and confined as mad, and the abbess blames Adriana for her husband’s supposed madness.

excerpt.locator: “The Comedy of Errors,” the other dinner explained through the abbess closing her gates; opens “When the married Antipholus was denied entrance into his own house (those within supposing him to be”; closes “r his recovery, and she retired into her house again, and ordered her gates to be shut against them.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the husband’s protest make his position worse?
facilitatorNotes: Adriana already assumes he is unwell, so his anger is treated as further proof rather than a reason to reconsider. The explanation absorbs the very evidence that should challenge it.
evidence: his rage only the more confirmed them in the belief

questions.prompt: What is valuable in the abbess’s first response, even though she does not yet know the truth?
facilitatorNotes: She offers shelter, questions the report and refuses immediate force. Pausing judgment protects the stranger from a mistaken accusation.
evidence: would not too hastily give up the man

questions.prompt: Does the abbess’s detailed explanation prove that jealousy caused madness?
facilitatorNotes: No: readers know twins caused the apparent contradictions. Her explanation is forceful and changes Adriana’s behaviour, but confident reasoning can still start from a false assumption.
evidence: your jealous fits have made your husband mad

days.title: Lamb’s Comedy of Errors: everyone in one place
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Explain how simultaneous evidence resolves what separate encounters could not.
days.focus: Recognition joins a public mystery to a private family history.
days.context: Ægeon’s deadline arrives as the disputes gather outside the convent. The reader now knows the cause of the confusion, but most characters still do not.
days.contentNote: The threatened execution is cancelled. References to enslavement and mental illness remain in the retelling.

excerpt.locator: “The Comedy of Errors,” sunset approaches through the tale’s ending; opens “During the course of this eventful day, in which so many errors had happened from the likeness the t”; closes “ one Dromio, be mistaken for the other, making altogether a pleasant and diverting Comedy of Errors.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Ægeon’s first recognition of a son fail to rescue him immediately?
facilitatorNotes: He sees the son separated from him in infancy, not the son who grew up with him. A real family relationship does not guarantee remembered recognition.
evidence: had never seen his father since they were separated in the storm

questions.prompt: What new evidence allows the duke to connect the morning story with the afternoon disputes?
facilitatorNotes: He sees both pairs together and remembers the shipwreck account. The shared appearance is finally evidence of two people rather than proof of one person’s inconsistency.
evidence: he remembered the story Ægeon had told him in the morning

questions.prompt: Why does the ending include the Dromios’ joy and the possibility of future blunders?
facilitatorNotes: Their reunion matters too, and the twins still look alike. The resolution restores relationships without unrealistically removing every occasion for confusion.
evidence: the two Dromios' humble joy must not be forgotten

days.title: October
days.challenge: Separate a wish to slow time from the more modest wish to change its felt speed.
days.focus: Attention, delay, and the vulnerability of a harvest.
days.context: The speaker addresses a mild autumn morning as if it could govern time, leaves, birds, and frost. Beguile can mean charm or pleasantly deceive; amethyst is a purple gemstone.

excerpt.locator:
October; source text begins "O hushed October morning mild,
Thy leaves have ripened to the fall;
To-morrow's wind, if it be " and ends "burnt with frost,
Whose clustered fruit must else be lost—
For the grapes' sake along the wall.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Boy%27s_Will/October

questions.prompt: What threatened changes make the mild morning precious?
facilitatorNotes: Wind may strip the leaves and crows may depart tomorrow. The present calm matters because it may not last.
evidence: To-morrow they may form and go.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask that the day seem less brief?
facilitatorNotes: The wording acknowledges perception: a day may feel longer through mist, color, and carefully noticed falling leaves, even if time does not stop.
evidence: Make the day seem to us less brief.

questions.prompt: How does the repeated appeal for the grapes alter the poem’s earlier requests?
facilitatorNotes: It adds a practical vulnerable crop to the desire for beauty and delay. Readers can consider whether concern for harvest and reluctance to lose autumn reinforce one another.
evidence: For the grapes' sake along the wall.

days.title: The Snow (1891 text)
days.challenge: Follow several image families without losing the single natural process they describe.
days.focus: Covering, leveling, and the disappearance of visible work.
days.context: Alabaster is pale stone; a sieve strains or sifts material; artisans are skilled workers. The title names the subject, but the poem itself keeps calling it it while shifting among household and clothing images.

excerpt.locator:
The Snow (1891 text); source text begins "IT sifts from leaden sieves,
It powders all the wood,
It fills with alabaster wool
The wrinkles" and ends " of posts,
As ankles of a queen,—
Then stills its artisans like ghosts,
Denying they have been.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems%3A_Second_Series_%28Dickinson%29/The_Snow

questions.prompt: How do sieves, powder, and wool make falling snow feel different?
facilitatorNotes: Sifting suggests fine falling particles, powder a coating, and wool a soft covering. Each image changes texture while retaining the same subject.
evidence: alabaster wool

questions.prompt: What is erased when mountain and plain acquire an even face?
facilitatorNotes: The cover reduces visible differences and hides the marks of roads and harvests. The poem imagines the landscape’s history becoming harder to read.
evidence: Acres of seams where harvests were

questions.prompt: Why end with artisans denying they have been there?
facilitatorNotes: Snow’s work becomes still and its agents invisible. The completed transformation remains although no worker can be seen, giving the ending a ghostly paradox.
evidence: Denying they have been.

days.title: Lamb’s Twelfth Night: a new name after a shipwreck
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Distinguish hope based on a witness’s report from certainty supplied later by the narrator.
days.focus: Disguise creates a route to safety and the conditions for future confusion.
days.context: Mary Lamb’s retelling follows Viola after she is separated from her twin Sebastian in a shipwreck.
days.contentNote: Includes shipwreck deaths and bereavement without graphic detail, and the narrator’s period judgments about suitable male and female behaviour.

excerpt.locator: “Twelfth Night, or What You Will,” opening through Cesario’s place at court; opens “Sebastian and his sister Viola, a young gentleman and lady of Messaline, were twins, and (which was ”; closes “no doubt his grave courtiers thought Cesario was for their once noble master, the great duke Orsino.”.

questions.prompt: What gives Viola reason to hope Sebastian survived, without proving it to her?
facilitatorNotes: The captain saw him supported on a mast before distance hid him. That is concrete evidence of survival at one moment, not knowledge of where he is now.
evidence: as long as he could see anything of him for the distance

questions.prompt: Why does Viola first wish to join Olivia’s household?
facilitatorNotes: Their grief for brothers seems to offer companionship and understanding. Olivia’s closed household blocks that first plan, prompting the alternative disguise.
evidence: who so tenderly mourned a brother's death

questions.prompt: How does the choice of clothing prepare the reader for later mistakes?
facilitatorNotes: Viola copies Sebastian’s usual colour and fashion, intensifying their resemblance. The narrator directly forecasts errors and confirms to readers that Sebastian also lived.
evidence: some strange errors happened by means of their being mistaken for each other

days.title: Lamb’s Twelfth Night: a messenger with an unspoken wish
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Read indirect speech for a meaning understood by the reader but missed by the listener.
days.focus: Duty and personal feeling pull the messenger in different directions.
days.context: Serving Orsino as the page Cesario, Viola hears his complaints about Olivia while quietly falling in love with him herself.
days.contentNote: Orsino claims that women cannot love as deeply as men, which Viola disputes, and insists on access after Olivia’s refusal.

excerpt.locator: “Twelfth Night, or What You Will,” Viola’s secret feeling through her first meeting with Olivia; opens “It is a dangerous matter for young maidens to be the confidants of handsome young dukes; which Viola”; closes “loved so long in vain, at first sight conceived a passion for the supposed page, the humble Cesario.”.

questions.prompt: How does Viola’s imagined case of a woman who loves Orsino challenge his demand on Olivia?
facilitatorNotes: It asks whether he could be required to return someone else’s love. He should then allow Olivia the same freedom to decline, though he rejects the comparison.
evidence: must she not be content with this answer?

questions.prompt: Why does the story of her father’s daughter let Viola speak both openly and secretly?
facilitatorNotes: She describes her own concealed affection as another woman’s history. Orsino hears a separate example; readers know the words reveal her present feelings.
evidence: she never told her love

questions.prompt: What double meaning does “I am not that which I play” carry?
facilitatorNotes: It sounds like a response about delivering a rehearsed speech, but also names her disguise as a male page. The conversation lets truth appear without full disclosure.
evidence: I am not that which I play

days.title: Lamb’s Twelfth Night: a ring changes the message
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Follow how an object exposes an intention and how a song carries different meanings for two listeners.
days.focus: A disguise can redirect feelings beyond the wearer’s plan.
days.context: Viola, disguised as Cesario, is meant to speak for Orsino, but Olivia has become interested in the messenger.
days.contentNote: The embedded song, printed under the heading SONG, uses a grave, a shroud and death as images of rejected love. The narrator’s period gender expectations are retained.

excerpt.locator: “Twelfth Night, or What You Will,” Olivia draws her veil through Viola’s answer about love; opens “When Viola asked to see her face, Olivia said: "Have you any commission from your lord and master to”; closes “ himself, and of a man's dark complexion; but Viola secretly meant Orsino, and not a woman like him.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Olivia’s praise of Orsino not contradict her refusal to marry him?
facilitatorNotes: She can recognise virtue, learning and rank without loving him. The speech separates admiration from an obligation to return affection.
evidence: yet I cannot love him

questions.prompt: What makes the ring useful evidence of Olivia’s real intention?
facilitatorNotes: Viola knows no ring was sent, so the claim about returning it is false. Combined with Olivia’s looks and manner, it suggests affection for Cesario.
evidence: knowing that Orsino had sent no ring by her

questions.prompt: How do Orsino and Viola hear the same love song from different positions?
facilitatorNotes: Both recognise unreturned love, but Viola’s beloved is listening beside her without knowing it. Her answer about age and complexion points to Orsino while he interprets it as a woman.
evidence: Viola secretly meant Orsino, and not a woman like him.

days.title: Lamb’s Twelfth Night: a stranger calls her Sebastian
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Track who sees which twin and how a mistaken accusation can carry useful information.
days.focus: Appearance creates conflict while also revealing a lost connection.
days.context: Olivia openly declares affection for Cesario. A jealous rival challenges the disguised Viola, and an unexpected helper enters.
days.contentNote: Includes threatened duels, exchanged blows and an arrest, without graphic wounds, and period claims that fear or courage belongs to one sex.

excerpt.locator: “Twelfth Night, or What You Will,” the second visit through Olivia welcoming Sebastian; opens “When Viola made her second visit to Olivia, she found no difficulty in gaining access to her. Servan”; closes “mpt and anger to be seen in his face, which she had complained of when she told her love to Cesario.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Viola’s second entrance into Olivia’s house easier than the first?
facilitatorNotes: The servants recognise their mistress’s interest and welcome the messenger. Social responses have changed even though Viola still carries Orsino’s unwanted suit.
evidence: the gates were thrown wide open

questions.prompt: How can Antonio’s accusation both wound Viola and give her hope?
facilitatorNotes: He mistakes her for the friend he rescued and believes she is ungrateful. Calling her Sebastian suggests her brother survived; the name supplies a different explanation for his anger.
evidence: she began to cherish hopes that it was her brother

questions.prompt: Why does Olivia read Sebastian’s willingness to enter as a change in Cesario?
facilitatorNotes: She assumes the same face means the same person and interprets a different response as improved affection. Readers know a new person, not a changed mind, explains it.
evidence: there was none of the contempt and anger to be seen in his face

days.title: Lamb’s Twelfth Night: two faces, one explanation
days.author: Mary Lamb
days.challenge: Resolve contradictory witness accounts and revisit earlier remarks with new knowledge.
days.focus: Recognition changes the meaning of facts already known.
days.context: Olivia has mistaken Sebastian for Cesario. Orsino, Viola and the arrested Antonio arrive before the two twins have met each other.
days.contentNote: Orsino threatens revenge, and Viola says she would accept death for him; the comic ending resolves the danger. The retelling laughs at Olivia’s mistaken attraction.

excerpt.locator: “Twelfth Night, or What You Will,” Sebastian agrees to marry through the tale’s ending; opens “Sebastian did not at all object to the fondness the lady lavished on him. He seemed to take it in ve”; closes “ino, the duke of Illyria, and Sebastian the husband of the rich and noble countess, the lady Olivia.”.

questions.prompt: Why do Antonio’s and Orsino’s three-month accounts appear impossible together?
facilitatorNotes: Each believes he knows the same youth, but one knows Sebastian and the other Viola. Both time claims can be true once the mistaken identity is corrected.
evidence: Three months has this youth attended on me

questions.prompt: Why is the priest’s truthful statement still misleading when applied to Viola?
facilitatorNotes: He witnessed Olivia marry Sebastian, whose appearance matches Viola’s disguise. Accurate testimony about an event becomes false identification when attached to the wrong person.
evidence: the evidence of that lady and the priest made Orsino believe

questions.prompt: How does learning Viola’s identity change Orsino’s understanding of earlier conversations?
facilitatorNotes: He recalls her statements of love as personal feeling rather than a page’s duty. The information is not new, but its interpretation changes; readers may also question how quickly his affection shifts.
evidence: many of her pretty sayings, which were like riddles to him

days.title: Good Hours
days.challenge: Infer a changed relationship to the same place from light and sound.
days.focus: Felt companionship, distance, and a return that cannot restore an earlier moment.
days.context: The speaker walks past a village on a winter evening and returns after the houses have gone dark. Profanation means an intrusion that feels disrespectful to something held sacred.

excerpt.locator:
Good Hours; source text begins "I had for my winter evening walk—
No one at all with whom to talk.
But I had the cottages in a " and ends " the slumbering village street
Like profanation, by your leave.
At ten o'clock of a winter eve.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/North_of_Boston/Good_Hours

questions.prompt: How can the speaker have company without someone walking alongside?
facilitatorNotes: Lit cottages, glimpsed faces, and a violin create an imagined relationship with people indoors. Thought signals that this is his perception.
evidence: And I thought I had the folk within

questions.prompt: Why does turning back fail to recover the earlier company?
facilitatorNotes: The windows have gone dark; time has passed as well as distance. The village is materially familiar but emotionally changed.
evidence: I saw no window but that was black.

questions.prompt: Why might the speaker compare creaking footsteps with profanation?
facilitatorNotes: His sound disturbs the sleeping street after its life has withdrawn. The strong religious word makes the discomfort greater than simple noise; alternatives should explain that disproportion.
evidence: Like profanation, by your leave,

days.title: As imperceptibly as grief (1891 text)
days.challenge: Hold conflicting emotional descriptions together without forcing a single mood.
days.focus: Gradual change and a departure imagined without ordinary means of travel.
days.context: Perfidy means betrayal; sequestered means secluded; a keel is the bottom structure of a boat. The speaker notices summer passing so gradually that its departure seems both gentle and painful.

excerpt.locator:

The summer lapsed away,—
Too imperceptible, at last,
To seem like per" and ends "hus, without a wing,

Our summer made her light escape

questions.prompt: Why compare summer’s disappearance with grief rather than a sudden storm?
facilitatorNotes: The change is gradual and difficult to notice while it happens. The comparison concerns its pace and felt passing, not a claim that all grief follows one pattern.
evidence: Too imperceptible, at last

questions.prompt: What tension lies in courteous yet harrowing grace?
facilitatorNotes: The departure seems polite and gentle while still distressing. The reluctant guest image allows both feelings to coexist.
evidence: As guest who would be gone

questions.prompt: How does leaving without wing or keel shape the last image?
facilitatorNotes: Summer needs neither flight nor a boat; its escape is a change of time and perception. Into the beautiful leaves the destination open rather than explaining it.
evidence: Into the beautiful.

days.title: Two Voyagers (1891 text)
days.challenge: Distinguish an observed disappearance from a story invented to follow it.
days.focus: Scale, uncertainty, and the limits of a witness’s knowledge.
days.context: Firmament and ether refer to sky; a frigate is a warship and a merchantman a trading ship. Two butterflies become travelers across an imagined sea of light.

excerpt.locator:
Two Voyagers (1891 text); source text begins "Two butterflies went out at noon
And waltzed above a stream,
Then stepped straight through the " and ends "en by the distant bird,
If met in ether sea
By frigate or by merchantman,
Report was not to me.". Scan-backed poem: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems:_Second_Series_(Dickinson)/Two_Voyagers

questions.prompt: What does waltzing make the butterflies’ movement seem like?
facilitatorNotes: It makes paired flight graceful and coordinated, like dancing, before their journey grows into a voyage.
evidence: waltzed above a stream

questions.prompt: How do beam and shining sea let a small flight become a much larger journey?
facilitatorNotes: Light becomes both a resting place and an ocean. The changing scale carries the butterflies beyond ordinary observation.
evidence: Upon a shining sea

questions.prompt: Does the final stanza say no one ever saw the butterflies again?
facilitatorNotes: No. It says any report did not reach this speaker. The distinction preserves uncertainty rather than making the observer all-knowing.
evidence: Report was not to me.
